rules.boundaries: Each accepted English xml:id and num label identify one complete chapter/paragraph citation unit. section is its stable paragraph ordinal within the book, never a Niese section.
rules.text: Exclude the verified num label together with its preceding whitespace; trim only running-text edge whitespace. Preserve every other original running character, punctuation and internal whitespace. No spelling repair or generated text.
rules.sourceIdentity: Retain each original English xml:id and its exact sameAs reference to the aligned Latin element. English text is extracted from its own source, not reconstructed from Latin.
rules.excludedBlocks: The complete TEI header, verified body release note and exact chapter/book headings are metadata outside running text. Their source evidence is retained.
rules.editorialMarkup: The accepted English paragraphs contain a leading num element and plain running text. Eight approved uncertainty notes are excluded from search and preserved in the source restoration ledger. No Latin additions, deletions, gaps or dagger representations are inherited. Unknown body markup stops extraction.
rules.phraseBoundaries: Physically consecutive paragraphs and chapters remain joinable in whole-book scope. The Prologue-to-Book-I transition has breakBefore=true. Phrases never cross books, works or editions.
rules.coordinates: All sourcePieces and section coordinates are zero-based original-text UTF-16 offsets, end exclusive. rawText includes the removed num label and its preceding whitespace; runningText excludes that prefix.
rules.readerRoute: /deh/?book={book}&chapter={chapter}&unit={paragraph}&english=pollard; chapter 0 is the Prologue and unit is chapter-local.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.1.1] In the first year after imperial rule had been conferred on Vespasian, Judaea was being torn apart by bitter wars and domestic seditions. It had enjoyed no respite from its woes even through the winter, when the savagery of wars usually rests.
paragraphs.runningText: In the first year after imperial rule had been conferred on Vespasian, Judaea was being torn apart by bitter wars and domestic seditions. It had enjoyed no respite from its woes even through the winter, when the savagery of wars usually rests.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.1.2] Indeed, a third tyrant, Eleazar, had joined the others, as though to correct the vices of his predecessors. Judas, Simon son of Ezeron, and Hezekiah, a young man of no low birth, conspired with him, and very many others accompanied them. They occupied the inner parts of the temple and stationed armed men all around above the doors, at the front of the vestibule itself. John, however, had the advantage in the number of his fellow conspirators and the multitude of his faction, but his position was lower. Although he took no rest and fought back against those above him, he was nevertheless hard pressed by having enemies above his head.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.1.3] Simon, whom the people had brought in as their tyrant, held the upper parts of the city; its lower parts too were filled with his people. The city suffered within itself from a threefold battle. There was no interruption, no rest, no truce; fighting went on at every moment. Many fell, countless men were slaughtered; blood flowed, fouled everything and filled the very thresholds of the temple. Corpses fell everywhere; some were struck by arrows, others by missiles. Of the three, John was in the middle, below Eleazar and above Simon. The advantage Eleazar had over him was the same advantage he himself had over Simon: his position between them meant that the more heavily he was pressed by one, the more he himself harmed the other. Better equipped than the others, however, with the support of engines and various kinds of weapons, he kept the war evenly balanced. Yet, besides those who waged war, many of the priests too were killed and sacrificed among the very victims they had slaughtered. For although a dense crop of missiles fell upon them all and battles raged everywhere, the priests still performed their solemn ministry of sacrifice and did not cease from the duty entrusted to them. The further inside the temple they were, the more severely they were struck down, because missiles driven by an engine delivered more violent blows. Many too who had come from the ends of the earth to pray, hoping for saving remedies, were caught in greater dangers the more closely they clung to the temple. You could see foreigners lying beside citizens, priests beside the profane, men of dignity beside the shameful, the self-indulgent beside the abstinent. The blood of all was mingled indiscriminately and ran like a torrent, pooling in the very innermost recesses of the temple; all around, the blood swelled, so that many champions of the factions, as they attacked one another, slipped on it and plunged into the blood, as though to sate their fury. Yet even then the tyrants’ followers were not frightened by the dangers into abandoning the battle. The greater the danger, the more fiercely the storm of fury raged. If destruction bore down more heavily on one side, the others pressed on more violently, as though towards victory, to destroy their disordered opponents.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.1.4] Eleazar or Simon could withdraw, so that they were separated by what amounted to truces, even if only for a few hours. John, however, was always under arms, at every moment in combat. If those above rested, those below on Simon’s side pressed him; if he drove these back, Eleazar assailed him. Nor did he himself allow them to remain at rest. When he had repelled one group, he sprang upon the other, ever watchful in combat and tireless in his very cruelty. When they spared their missiles, they hurled fire, which caught the rooftops and devoured the houses. These were filled with grain and other stores of food for enduring a prolonged war; they too were burnt, providing greater fuel for the conflagration. Charred timbers fell; the tops of lofty buildings came crashing down.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.1.5] Thus bloodshed, fire, ruin and famine severed the sinews of the whole city. No place was free of danger, no time could be found for counsel; there was no hope of a change, no opportunity for escape. Everything was mournful, full of horror, full of savagery: everywhere grief and terror, everywhere the cries of women, the wailing of old men, the groans of the dying, the despair of the living. You would have called those who remained pitiable, those who had died blessed.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.2.1] How you have been deceived, city, by your peoples, through whom you once seemed blessed! How you have been stormed by your own arms, and your own hands turned against you—you who used to conquer without arms and strike the enemy without any battle, when angels fought for you and the waves of the sea, the chasms of the earth and the crashes of heaven served in your army! Arise now, Moses, and see your nation and the inheritance of the people entrusted to you perishing by their own hands. Look upon that people of God, for whom the sea opened a path as they walked, for whom heaven supplied food when they were hungry: they are shut in without a sea, besieged without a Pharaoh, starving without any barrenness of the land. Arise, Aaron, who once, when death was devouring very many of the people because they had offended almighty God, stood between the living and the dead: death stood still, and the plague was checked by the barrier of your body and could not pass on to infect the living. Awaken, you too, Joshua son of Nun, who levelled the impregnable walls of Jericho as the priests sounded their trumpets, and see the people to whom you subjected foreigners now themselves subjected and oppressed. Awaken, David, who used to drive out the tormenting spirit by the sweetness of the lyre, and see how fury rules and has erased all the sweetness of your psalms from the minds of the lost. Each of their leaders offers the whole people to death to wrest away their freedom—the people for whom you offered yourself to death. Awaken, Elisha, who brought the enemy into Samaria and made him a friend. Through you the crash of four-horse chariots rang out in the camp of Syria, the sound of horsemen and the sound of an army; the enemy fled, the Jew escaped the siege. Where now are those merits, where now those works of the saints? Nor is it surprising that they have lost the works of the prophets, since they denied the master of the prophets. Therefore your own arms are turned against you, Judaea; your prayers avail you nothing, because your faith accomplishes nothing. Therefore your people have turned against you, because your faithlessness has turned back upon you. What remedy can be sought where the author of the remedy is not reconciled? What did you think would happen when with your own hands you crucified your salvation, when with your own hands you extinguished your life, when with your own voices you drove out your advocate, when by your own assaults you killed your helper, except that you would lay your own hands upon yourself as well? You have what you asked for. You deprived yourself of the guardian of peace; you asked that the master of life be killed and that Barabbas be granted to you, who had been sent to prison for sedition committed in the city and for murder. Therefore salvation has departed from you, peace has gone, rest has ceased; sedition has been given to you, destruction has been given. Acknowledge that for you today Barabbas lives, Jesus is dead. Therefore sedition reigns within you, peace lies buried, so that you perish more cruelly at the hands of your own than if you perished at the hands of foreigners. What evil did the Roman bring upon you with his arms, wretched city, that equalled what your own people brought? It was your own people who made you fight the Romans. The Romans wanted peace; you declared war. What reason was there to provoke those stronger than you? It was certainly grievous that a gentile entered the temple contrary to the sacred law; but it was no longer God’s temple. You were not God’s city, nor could you be, because you were the tomb of the dead, and above all of your own people whom you yourself had killed, not those you had lost to the enemy. For how could you be the dwelling of life when you were the habitation of death, a lodging for crimes, a cave of brigands? Ananus and Jesus, chief priests, lay unburied within you. Those who had so recently been clothed in priestly robes and had been held in reverence even by foreigners lay as disfigured corpses, food for birds and a meal for dogs, their limbs torn and scattered throughout the city. The very image of ancient holiness seemed to lament so great an insult to the sacred name and the disfigurement of an office once glorious. But you yourself began this indignity, you who killed the prophets in your very bosom, who stoned the saints of the Lord. Zechariah lay lifeless before the temple; he lay unburied. Thus this blood washes away that blood. And what caused Ananus’s death except that he rebuked your people for not rising in defence of the temple, and protested that freedom had been betrayed, valour abandoned, the remnants of the ancient sacred rites trampled upon and the altars defiled? He declared that the people should be abandoned: like unfeeling images and statues of marble, they no longer felt anything. For dumb animals are accustomed at least to retaliate in vengeance, to feel an injury, to be stirred by a goad, to avoid blows. Whoever, then, is neither stirred nor knows how to avoid what harms him is like things without feeling. And indeed, where is that freedom of yours, from zeal for which you once thought you must yield neither to the Egyptians, nor to the Palestinians, nor to the Assyrians, nor later to the Medes? Where is that faith of the Maccabees which once, with a few men, routed the Babylonians, put the Persians to flight and struck down Demetrius, and at last, in little children and women, overcame Antiochus’s arms, swords and fires, and preferred to die for ancestral observance rather than obey the king’s commands? Where is that devotion of the fathers, the most beautiful of all sufferings, by which they offered themselves to death no more for their children and wives than for God’s temple? Once even the priestly rod blossomed, cut from a wild root; now faith itself is dry, devotion is buried, and all emulation of valour has departed. Nor is it surprising that a people who have withdrawn from God and follow the wicked spirit of contradiction are divided against themselves. For how could they preserve their own peace when they rejected the peace of God? The peace of God is Christ, who made both one. Rightly, then, from one people they became many hostile to one another, because they would not follow Jesus, who unites what is divided, but followed the spirit of fury, who divides what is united. You were therefore paying the price of your faithlessness, Jerusalem, when with your own hands you destroyed your defences, when with your own blades you pierced your entrails, so that the enemy pitied you, so that he spared you while you raged. For he saw that God was fighting against you and taking the Romans’ part, so that you brought voluntary betrayal upon yourself. Therefore the Romans preferred to be spectators rather than killers, lest laying a hand upon your entrails as they raged against one another be judged a matter of contamination rather than courage. To these torments of abominable slaughter was added the enormity of impious cruelty: they denied burial to all who had been killed either in the temple or around the city’s streets. No one had leisure to bury anyone while they were occupied in war against one another, and the concern to strike rather than to bury possessed them all. Thus in a kind of fury they had killed the duties of devotion, while the services of impiety grew savage. In so many calamities nothing had perished more completely than mercy, which alone is accustomed to lighten misery and console suffering. For those who had lost their own people did not dare to bury them out of fear, since grievous terror threatened them from the leaders of the opposing faction; and those who had killed others took care that no one snatched them away for burial. Thus everyone had to fear that what he wished to grant another he would receive himself, or, worse still, that he himself would not obtain the use of a tomb which he had prepared for another. In the temple itself, therefore, instead of sweet-smelling ointments, instead of fragrant censers, instead of the scents of various flowers, there was the heavy stench of unburied corpses, dissolved by rain, scorched by flame, heated by the sun. Every limb of the slaughtered citizens reeked with a dreadful smell. On one side the putrefaction of decaying entrails, on the other the fumes of burnt bodies filled all the senses and mouths of the living, so that they themselves were soon consumed by a more grievous disease. They groaned that they had survived to perish by a harsher punishment, and had been preserved to see the laws of nature dissolved together with their fatherland: justice denied to the living, peace to citizens, burial to the dead; human and divine things alike stained and polluted; everything confounded; mercy made criminal, cruelty counted as religion. A camp in the temple, war on the threshold, a funeral upon the altars: they saw with their own eyes what they had not believed would come when the prophets announced it. Had not David spoken of them: “They polluted your holy temple; they made the mortal remains of your servants food for the birds of heaven; they poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them”? For at that time the nations came into God’s inheritance to carry everything away, and at the same time the temple was polluted by the deaths of its own people, and the corpses of the slain lay unburied as food for birds, for the voracity of beasts. Blood was poured out until it pooled in the temple; there was no one to bury them, because fury passed from the living to the dead, and from the dead to those who still lived. Someone wished to bury a dead man and was himself killed; the man who had killed the dead man turned his anger upon the one who would bury him, killing the latter to deny the former burial. Again, the man who killed the would-be burier practised greater cruelty upon the dead man, depriving one who now owed nothing to hatred and felt no torments of nature’s final due. What else could happen to those who did not receive the divine oracles? They mocked the prophets’ announcements, trampled upon all sacred law, and did not believe that the things would happen which they themselves hastened to bring about. For there was an ancient and often-repeated saying that the city of Jerusalem would perish and its sacred things be burnt when sedition invaded the law of war and domestic hands defiled God’s temple. They did not understand even this. How often had God’s house been destroyed, how often had there been sedition, how often a siege, how often war! That city never perished except when they truly crucified God’s temple with domestic hands. And let them hear what temple that was: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall raise it up.” For what else was it but sacrilege when they stretched out impious hands against the author of salvation, when they stoned him, when they struck him, when they seized him, when they killed him? Then divine fire truly consumed their sacred things. For those things had been burnt by the Babylonians and afterwards repaired, destroyed by Pompey and restored again; but when Jesus came they were burnt away completely, and, dissolved by the heat of the divine Spirit, vanished.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.2.2] It was necessary for us, with a somewhat fuller lament, to lead what was, as it were, the funeral of our ancestral observance, to accompany a kind of funeral procession and pay the last duties to the institutions of our forebears. But let us come to the beginnings of the siege of Jerusalem.

But let us come to the beginnings of the siege of Jerusalem.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.3.1] Titus had returned to Judaea. After an interval of a few days, to fill the ranks of the military units from which a picked force had been sent to Italy, he fanned the war into flame, hastening to accompany his father so as not to send him alone into danger to fight against the forces of Vitellius. He therefore set out with his army in splendid array, the column alert and ready everywhere, suspecting ambushes because he saw that he had the advantage in valour. He came through the territory of Samaria. Gophna received him, having long since gone over to the Romans. They reached Aulona, from which Jerusalem was thirty stades away and no more. From there he took six hundred horsemen and rode before the city, also to reconnoitre the lie of the land, the nature of the fortifications, the height of the walls and the disposition of the common people. They were said to be oppressed by the brigands’ arms and hemmed in by the mass of the factions, so that they unwillingly submitted to the siege and were prevented from making known their disposition towards the Romans, as they would if given freedom. He therefore rode in conspicuous splendour with a few horsemen along the public road leading to the city walls, and no one was seen to come out.
paragraphs.runningText: Titus had returned to Judaea. After an interval of a few days, to fill the ranks of the military units from which a picked force had been sent to Italy, he fanned the war into flame, hastening to accompany his father so as not to send him alone into danger to fight against the forces of Vitellius. He therefore set out with his army in splendid array, the column alert and ready everywhere, suspecting ambushes because he saw that he had the advantage in valour. He came through the territory of Samaria. Gophna received him, having long since gone over to the Romans. They reached Aulona, from which Jerusalem was thirty stades away and no more. From there he took six hundred horsemen and rode before the city, also to reconnoitre the lie of the land, the nature of the fortifications, the height of the walls and the disposition of the common people. They were said to be oppressed by the brigands’ arms and hemmed in by the mass of the factions, so that they unwillingly submitted to the siege and were prevented from making known their disposition towards the Romans, as they would if given freedom. He therefore rode in conspicuous splendour with a few horsemen along the public road leading to the city walls, and no one was seen to come out.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.3.2] But when he turned his horse aside to go around the circuit of the walls, with the rest of the troop following their commander, very many suddenly burst out from the place called Opposite Helena’s Tomb and leapt forward to occupy the road, cutting off the greater part of the horsemen following Titus. He himself had passed by with a few men, as the ambushers had deliberately allowed, so that they could more easily overpower him when he was left unsupported by the rest. For it was not easy to return to his men because of the mass of enemies thrust between them, while a ditch or rampart and the other obstacles of the terrain prevented him from going further forward, bringing danger upon him on both sides.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.4.1] Seeing, therefore, that his only remedy for safety lay in valour, and that a path must be opened by the sword and by no other means—for the others had already turned their horses and withdrawn, hoping that the emperor’s son too would follow—he turned his horse. Shouting to encourage the rest to follow him, he charged upon the enemy. It would seem impossible to explain how he could have escaped, were it not known that boldness has very great power in war and is a wall in itself, even when alone. Moreover, with others following behind him, the worthless rabble thought they should look to their own safety in danger rather than pursue the enemy; and anyone who stretched out a hand to seize his horse was struck down. In the end, only two of Titus’s companions were killed, and the emperor’s son returned to his men with the rest. Nor indeed does there seem to be any doubt why, although his head was uncovered and the rest of him unprotected, he received no wound even when the missiles were being aimed chiefly at him. He had gone out on a ride, not prepared for battle, and had put on neither helmet nor breastplate: so great a man was being preserved for the destruction of that city. The king’s heart is indeed, is indeed in the hand of God.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.4.2] Therefore, lest the success of their deceit and the progress of their trickery increase the Jews’ boldness, he returned to the city with his army after the night. From a lookout from which the city and the vast expanse of the temple could be seen, he showed his men what sort of city they had to fight. They must be tireless and more cautious, since they had to overcome an innumerable people prepared for deceit. He arranged which ranks should approach the walls; those he knew were still exhausted by the night’s march he stationed at a distance as reserves. They advanced gradually.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.4.3] When they reached the Mount of Olives, beneath it a valley called Cedron lay between their route and the city. Seeing from the walls that the army had been stationed there, for it was six stades away, the Jews laid aside their zeal for sedition for a time. With external enemies approaching, a domestic compact suspended their civil struggles. For fear often restrains even bitter hatred. Accordingly, the men of the factions encouraged one another to defend their fatherland with a common resolve, lest their discord give the Romans a bloodless victory. Relying on their numbers, they decided to attack the enemy suddenly, and by an unexpected sortie threw the foremost ranks into confusion. But when the Romans, trained by long experience itself and by battles of many kinds, had steadied their spirits, they stood firm in their formation and began to cut down the attackers, repel them with shields and drive them back with volleys of missiles, though by no means without destruction on both sides. The Jews had almost overwhelmed them and the Roman battle line was wavering, when Titus learnt what was happening and arrived. Meeting the adversaries and strengthening his men, he renewed the battle and raised the soldiers’ spirits, rebuking the Roman ranks for yielding victory to a disordered multitude, a thing that could not be done without the reproach of the greatest cowardice. Having repelled the Jews, who were pursuing even those separated from them by the valley, he returned victorious to his men. Confident in the support the higher position afforded against those below, if they tried to engage, he turned to another part of the Roman army.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.4.4] As Caesar departed, the Jews poured out from the walls and charged upon the enemy in a great column, so that at the onrush of the innumerable multitude the soldiers fled and withdrew to the higher parts of the hills. With their flank exposed, even the others who would have preferred battle fled. Meanwhile Caesar stood in their midst. Very many begged him not to expose himself to danger and, with the army scattered, bear the whole danger alone, since he was master of the world: he should no longer fight as before in the role of a soldier, but in that of an emperor, whose danger meant destruction for all. He did not yield. Placing military honour before safety, and judging a glorious death to outweigh the disgrace of life, he presented his breast to the enemy. When he had terrified those he had advanced against, he turned upon others. By his appearance alone and the renown of his all too well-known and eager courage he drove back the enemy. Those he approached therefore gave way, but from other quarters the Jews poured in more and more. They had almost surrounded Titus when very many soldiers, seeing Caesar in the midst of the battle, cried out to the rest, signalling that the emperor’s son must not be abandoned in danger. Thus shame recalled them all, and fear armed them, lest they be branded with the disgrace of having deserted Caesar. Turning upon the Jews, they drove the disordered multitude into the valley with all their strength and valour; nor was it difficult for those ascending to slip back. Thus Titus twice recalled the fleeing military unit from flight and freed it alike from danger and disgrace. He displayed equal valour on both occasions, and at the last employed shame as well: by shunning cowardice, shame brought valour, first so that Caesar should not be abandoned, and then so that the enemy should be driven back.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.5.1] When the battle outside had subsided for a little while, the internal battle took its place. For at the arrival of the Passover festival, John enlisted very many men to approach the temple as though for religious observance, and contrived a trap when they were allowed to enter as allies. They entered in civilian guise but armed beneath their clothing; throwing off their garments, they raised their swords, their breasts armoured and themselves girded with protection for battle. Struck with terror, those inside the temple who were attending the festival unarmed rushed out and left the temple empty. As the intruders followed them, slaughtering those they could catch and pursuing others beyond the temple precinct, John and his companions were given the opportunity to break in.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.5.2] Many people were slaughtered there, so that even those who had not resisted were killed on some fabricated charges. The tranquillity of peace did not help them, nor silence those who kept quiet, nor patience those who yielded. Having seized the inner parts of the temple, John rode down upon Simon as well, with Eleazar and the other leaders of the third faction appointed beneath him to a secondary position.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.6.1] Titus advanced against the enemy for a third time and led out his army. On his arrival he encountered a dense multitude of Jews before the city, giving the appearance of wishing to surrender to the Romans but seeming afraid. Suspecting a trick, especially because he had recently seen them united and obstinate, he did not think it credible that they had suddenly changed. He warned the soldiers to guard against deceit and not rashly to approach the walls except at his command, in a close column, lest those who had come out of the city surround them from behind. Suddenly a sound rang out from the city, and a kind of disturbance echoed softly, as some pretended to be leaving of their own accord and others even resisted them: the former demanded that the gates be opened to them, the latter ordered them kept shut; some wished for peace, others for war.

On his arrival he encountered a dense multitude of Jews before the city, giving the appearance of wishing to surrender to the Romans but seeming afraid. Suspecting a trick, especially because he had recently seen them united and obstinate, he did not think it credible that they had suddenly changed. He warned the soldiers to guard against deceit and not rashly to approach the walls except at his command, in a close column, lest those who had come out of the city surround them from behind. Suddenly a sound rang out from the city, and a kind of disturbance echoed softly, as some pretended to be leaving of their own accord and others even resisted them: the former demanded that the gates be opened to them, the latter ordered them kept shut; some wished for peace, others for war.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.6.2] The mass of the soldiers rushed forward to assist those who had called from the walls for help. Very many went beyond their orders without formation or any restraint, as though to meet those approaching and bring assistance: with help nearer at hand, more people might be given confidence to break out, or those resisting might be frightened, or the soldiers themselves might have an opportunity to break through those who resisted. Those standing outside began to surround them from behind and press upon them once encircled. They took refuge, as it were, at the wall, suspecting nothing from those who made a show of peace. From there too stones and missiles were hurled down, and suddenly the pretence of peace turned into battle. Roused by this, they ran back against the enemies who, although they had tried to surround the Roman soldiers who had advanced, themselves feared being surrounded by the whole army. Thus, while guarding against the whole army, the Jews let these men slip almost from their hands, though they had already considered them captured. They had inflicted very many wounds, but most of them had themselves been wounded as well. They nevertheless pursued them as far as Helena’s tomb and, as is customary for men taunting their opponents, clashed their shields, mocking the Romans because they had now trapped them in ambushes for the second time.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.7.1] Caesar, considerably angered, forbade the returning men to mingle with the rest and summoned an assembly, saying: “Great though Roman valour is, surpassing the peoples of all nations, it excels above all in orderly disposition and obedience to orders. For this is the safeguard of military discipline. Nor is it surprising that the Jews weave plots and devise deceits, since they judge themselves unequal in courage. But just as it is the part of the weaker to rely on ambushes, so it is the part of the stronger to guard against deceit making a mockery of valour.” He therefore marvelled that they could act in agreement in their desperation, while the Romans could not agree as their circumstances improved, with the result that the success of the enemy’s deceit stood on firm ground, while their own attempts at valour remained uncertain. “But if the enemy’s courage were stronger, rather than their deceit superior, it would be less disgraceful. For to be defeated by equals or stronger men brings no reproach. Yet when there is nothing to find fault with in you except your lack of restraint in fighting and a certain hasty intemperance of your hands, what can be more shameful than to reject military discipline in Caesar’s presence? I think the laws of military service themselves groan greatly at the disgrace of such indiscipline, and that the emperor will groan greatly when he learns of it. He has always preferred to be obeyed by his own soldier rather than feared by the enemy. For a soldier’s obedience hastens success; the enemy’s fear delays victory.” He asked what judgement his father would pass on his son, whose command was held in so little esteem by the army. “For judgement is pronounced upon a commander whose order is disregarded, and there is no doubt that punishment has more often been inflicted upon those who fought the enemy contrary to orders than upon those who advanced according to orders and yielded to valour. For the laws prescribe death for a man who leaves his formation. What, then, will happen where not one man but the army everywhere leaves its formation and neglects its commander’s decision? Know that you are soldiers of the Roman dominion, the people and the senate, among whom even to have won without the authority of an order is a crime.”

paragraphs.rawText: [V.7.2] With a speech of this kind he terrified not only the officers of the soldiers but the whole army as well. For, since he attacked the leaders of the ranks themselves more fiercely, he seemed about to punish everyone. All therefore gathered around him and begged that the fault of the few who had first abandoned their duty should be forgiven for the sake of them all. Although Caesar was not quick to pardon the offence, he was not impervious to appeals for indulgence. He granted it with the utmost gravity, saying that he was pardoning them all and that the authority of his rebuke had sufficiently punished them all. For punishment of individuals should proceed to action, but punishment of a multitude only to words: the former as far as a penalty, the latter as far as a rebuke. Setbacks in battle, he said, had often given good armies occasions for future deeds of valour.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.8.1] After this Titus turned his anger against the enemy. Considering that a siege among so many precipices and sheer slopes was dangerous, since soldiers taken unawares by sudden sorties would have no place to retreat to, from which to rush upon the enemy, or in which to set up engines, he ordered the precipices before the city to be filled in. While this was being done, the Jews were by no means free of the dangers of the moment. They were being afflicted by domestic battle while the Romans were occupied in filling the precipices.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.8.2] Neither side had a small force. Ten thousand men were with Simon, and fifty commanders over them. About five thousand Idumaeans also supported Simon’s side, under Jacob and the younger Simon. John, however, having occupied the inner parts of the temple by the deceit we described above, was kindling the war with a following of six thousand armed men. Two thousand, with a further four hundred men, joined him after they had begun to unite with their aims in accord for the defence of the city, under Eleazar and Simon son of Arinus, whom they had had as leaders before. As these men fought one another, the people lay between them as the victors’ prey and were transferred this way and that, like the prize of the contest, according to its changing outcome. For a little while they had come to an agreement, in the manner of a truce, and had been roused by the first Roman assault. With their entrails diseased, they fell back into their old sickness of internal fever whenever the onset of external maladies grew less severe. Often there was war outside and sedition within, the latter now all the more grievous because sedition itself was nourished by war and nourished war. Two men contended for power; the people between them were anxious not about slavery, but lest they fall to a worse master.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.9.1] A powerful man of the Canaanites founded the city of Jerusalem. In his native language he was called the just king. He first named it Solyma; afterwards he added a temple, whence the city was called Hierosolyma. From the beginning its inhabitants were of the Canaanite nation. David was the first man of the Hebrew nation to drive out the Canaanites and establish his own people there; he built himself a royal house in the city. He also wished to found a temple for God, but, forbidden by an oracle, he left Solomon as his heir to build the temple he himself had wished to build. Solomon therefore founded the temple, and the kings each added very many things to adorn the city.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.9.2] Envy arose from its magnificence. Among all its works, however, the temple excelled in its immense construction and gleaming marble. Within it was a precious and very large curtain woven with scarlet, blue, fine linen and purple. Material of such diversity was not without purpose: its appearance signified the mysteries of hidden things, because it was the temple of him who, as creator of the elements, had dominion over heaven and air, earth and sea, and alone ruled and governed all things. For scarlet represented the fiery heaven, blue the air, fine linen the earth because it grows in it, and purple the sea because it is dyed with sea shellfish. Thus you may infer two from their colour and two from their origin.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.9.3] Accordingly, the chief priest was accustomed to express these four things in his clothing when the greatest celebration of the festival days took place, as though putting on the whole world as he was about to make supplication for the people. He was a figure of him who was to come, Jesus, chief priest, to take away the sin of the world. The chief priest covered his thighs underneath with a linen garment, because faith of mind and chastity of body are sought above all in a priest, and chastity should gird up the intemperance of the flesh. There were two sacred tabernacles, one inner and the other outer. The priests always entered the outer one, but into the inner one, which was called the second, only the chief priest entered, once, and not without blood, to offer it for himself and for the people’s offence. By this the Holy Spirit signified that Jesus would come, who alone would truly enter the innermost recesses of the divine mysteries and, because he knew all the secrets of the heavenly substance, alone also reconcile the whole world to the Father through his own blood, so as to have mercy on things both heavenly and earthly. Accordingly, after he came, he made all things peaceful through the blood of his cross, whether they are on earth or in heaven.

The chief priest covered his thighs underneath with a linen garment, because faith of mind and chastity of body are sought above all in a priest, and chastity should gird up the intemperance of the flesh. The priests always entered the outer one, but into the inner one, which was called the second, only the chief priest entered, once, and not without blood, to offer it for himself and for the people’s offence. By this the Holy Spirit signified that Jesus would come, who alone would truly enter the innermost recesses of the divine mysteries and, because he knew all the secrets of the heavenly substance, alone also reconcile the whole world to the Father through his own blood, so as to have mercy on things both heavenly and earthly. Accordingly, after he came, he made all things peaceful through the blood of his cross, whether they are on earth or in heaven.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.9.4] Within was the incense burner, within the table, within the lamp. The incense burner signified that the prayer of the chief priest is directed to God the Father like incense; the table, that on it are Christ’s suffering and the mysteries of the sacraments. Hence David also says, “You have prepared a table in my sight”: its twelve loaves, as it were, are the twelve apostles, witnesses of his suffering and resurrection. The lamp, which is placed upon the lampstand, was formerly under a bushel, that is, under the measure of the law; now it is in the fullness of grace, pouring forth abundant light from seven wicks, because the Holy Spirit illuminates God’s temple with the powers of the seven greatest graces. Knowledge of the Trinity was therefore in the inner parts of the temple, which were called the holy of holies. There Aaron’s rod, once laid away, blossomed, for priestly grace in Christ would accomplish more after the death by which he redeemed the world. Before the temple were fourteen steps, by which the shadow had ascended in the time of King Hezekiah, signifying to him that the end of his life was to come. But, warned by an oracle, he prayed and obtained a delay of death, with this sign: the sun moved back over the same steps, signifying that an extension of life of the same number of years had been granted him.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.10.1] Since the city was thus fortified on every side by the works of very many kings, and especially of Herod, who had fortified the stronghold called Antonia with construction of the greatest magnificence and adorned it with the most splendid beauty, Caesar went around it, seeking the point at which he could most easily pour his forces into the city. After inspecting the wall’s whole circuit, he judged that the siege should be begun near the mound where John, chief priest, lay buried. As he explored more carefully, Nicanor, one of his friends who stayed close to him and applied himself earnestly to the task, was struck by an arrow and fell. He had approached nearer because he thought there would be some prospect of future peace if he were given an opportunity to open a conversation; he was considered powerful and effective in speech at influencing his hearers’ minds. Caesar was angered that they had inflicted death by an unexpected wound on a man who was urging what would save them. He drove his columns into battle, and war blazed up with the hurling of weapons of various kinds, especially missiles. Battering rams were brought up to strike the strong parts of the walls.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.10.2] Alarmed by this, all who had previously contended with one another in their pursuit of domination came together in concord. Granting impunity for past deeds, they made themselves one body and, united under the compulsion of danger, defended the city. Advancing also to the mounds, they hurled fire upon the engines to destroy the siege banks, burn the siege shelters and set fire to the rams.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.10.3] They would have burnt almost every kind of engine had not very many picked soldiers and allies, especially those from the region of Alexandria, fought back vigorously. Although these resisted strongly, Caesar gave them the additional aid of more powerful horsemen. Fighting fiercely himself, he struck down twelve champions of the opposing column. Thus the mass of the remaining multitude withdrew into the city to avoid destruction, and the Roman works were defended from the fire. John, leader of the Idumaeans, fell in that battle. While conversing before the walls with a Roman soldier known to him, he was struck in the back by an arrow and immediately collapsed. An Arab, one of the most skilful marksmen, is said to have caused his death. The Idumaeans, it is said, were deeply grieved because they had lost a man both ready in action and sound in counsel.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.11.1] The following night it happened that three towers which Titus had ordered to be raised upon the siege bank, so that he could strike the Jews with darts either from the same level or from above, suddenly collapsed without any force from the enemy. The noise threw the whole Roman army into confusion. They believed that the enemy had destroyed the siege banks and undermined the towers, whose fall had spread immense wreckage far and wide. A pitiable disgrace almost occurred: the victors would have yielded in flight to enemies whose presence was uncertain in the night. But the darkness and the collapse itself, which raised a cloud of dust, had taken away their view, so that they did not know where to flee. Each man asked his neighbour what had happened, but could obtain no reliable account, since everyone was equally ignorant of the cause of such a collapse. At last Caesar learnt the facts and ordered it to be made known that what had happened was a sudden accident, not an incursion by any enemy.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.11.2] Thus the alarm subsided, and the capture of the city depended entirely on force. For the walls were very high, much of them was covered with iron or bronze, and their very height protected the enemy from missiles. The Romans brought up the engines of the battering rams, whose repeated blows loosened the strong parts of the wall. They began to rely on lighter darts and arrows to drive off the defenders and overcome the hindrance of those resisting them. Thus the wall gradually yielded to their battering. Hence the Jews called the larger ram itself the destroyer of cities. When part of the walls had been broken down, the Jews abandoned that wall’s defences, confident that they had two other walls within, and withdrew to the second wall. As they fled, the Romans entered through the openings in the wall and opened the gates. Thus the whole army was admitted and completely demolished the outer wall, so that it would not obstruct them in battle or, if matters went badly, bar their retreat.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.12.1] The fellow conspirators of John and Simon divided the positions around the second wall between them. John fought with his men in the stronghold called Antonia. Near it was the portico of the temple which faced north. For the site itself, lying between two porticoes, where the stronghold was later built to bear Antony’s name, was called northern, that is, borius. Simon had taken on the duty of defending the city at John’s tomb. These men fought for safety, the Romans for victory. Although the Romans had superior valour for combat, their position was inferior for conducting the siege, since fighting from the wall bore heavily upon them.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.12.2] The Jews’ rashness was more insolent, the Romans’ courage more fierce. The commanders watched over their sides, and rivalry grew all the greater as each man longed to prove to his own leaders the dangers he faced. Simon pressed his men with terror and fear; Titus appealed to the Romans above all through their sense of shame before him. They thought it worse than death not to display before Caesar the dangers they faced, when he himself had so often not hesitated to expose himself to danger for the army. The habit of winning and ignorance of yielding armed them, and especially Titus’s presence as judge of each man’s valour. They did not look to him for a reward for courage: beyond all else, to have done something vigorous under his gaze that did not displease him was itself the richest reward. Spurred by this, Longinus, a man of the cavalry, saw the opposing bands of Jews before the walls. As though indignant that they should challenge the Romans to war and dare to come out on equal terms, he leapt from his horse and flung himself into the midst of the enemy. He struck one man who was preparing to meet him in the mouth with a weapon, taking his voice and life together. Tearing the weapon from the fallen body, he drove it into another man and returned victorious to his own side. We speak of the outstanding men; there were many imitators on both sides, but of different kinds. Despair gave the Jews boldness; desire for glory added valour to the Romans. Yet, though their spirits differed, their contempt for death was equal. The Jews thought it a consolation to die with the enemy. Titus hastened to finish the war, but without loss of his own men; he preferred to save even the enemies themselves, if he could save them all, rather than destroy them. He urged the soldier only to wage war with deliberation: the only true valour was that which had foresight as its companion; courage without judgement seemed rashness, and nowhere was greater caution needed than in victory. For to perish with the stronger man was a triumph for the defeated. Care must therefore be taken lest victory seem a matter of chance, and failure to escape sharing the danger a matter of cowardice. He therefore ordered the ram to be brought up to the middle of the northern wall.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.13.1] There was Castor, cunning and ready for deceit, who held the position with nine other partners in deceit after the rest had been driven away by the archers’ missiles. When he saw that the ram’s impact was overturning the tower, that the wall was tottering and would easily fall if the engine struck again, he stretched out his hands and begged Caesar in a pitiable voice to spare the city now on the brink of ruin and not resolve to bring it down in utter destruction. Caesar thought that he was earnestly begging pardon and would surrender. To allow the surrender to proceed, he ordered the engine to stop and the marksmen to refrain from battle. He gave Castor leave to speak. Castor pretended that he would come down and then seemed to persuade his men. Some were willing, others resisted; suddenly, as though indignant at being compelled, they struck themselves above the parapet and fell. There was great amazement, while the deceit remained hidden. Thus they drew out the time.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.13.2] Meanwhile, one of the Roman soldiers struck Castor’s nostril with an arrow. Castor lamented and complained to Caesar, demanding that he order someone to give him his right hand; on those terms he would come over. Caesar entrusted the task to Josephus, but he, knowing the Jews’ ambushes, replied that he perceived nothing sincere in it. Aeneas, however, approached nearer the wall and came forward to receive Castor as he came down. Castor shouted to him to open the fold of his garment and receive gold, then dropped a stone. Aeneas, keeping a watchful eye, saw the stone beforehand and escaped with a swift sideways leap. Yet the huge falling stone overwhelmed another man standing nearby. At this Caesar pressed more fiercely for the walls’ destruction, ordering the engine to be driven forward with greater force. In reply, fire was hurled to burn the engines. But when the wall broke apart, Castor and his men threw themselves as though into the fire, deceitfully displaying greatness of spirit in contempt for death, while by shameful deceit he sought a means of escape to preserve his life.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.14.1] Only one wall, the third, now remained, two having been overthrown. Yet Caesar still maintained his patience, realising that whatever perished was now a loss to himself. While sparing them and inviting them to surrender, he rushed upon the second wall with a few men without waiting for his column. The Jews gathered a force and wounded very many men in the narrow passages. Many also died on both sides. Then Caesar shot at those resisting from a distance with arrows. Among the crowded ranks no missile could be evaded; no shot failed to wound. Thus the Jews began to withdraw, and Titus recovered his men. Famine had already begun to press heavily upon the city.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.14.2] The Jews, however, boasted as victors because they had recovered the second wall, as though they had driven out the Romans. But they could neither repair what had fallen nor defend what was about to fall. They nevertheless resisted for a little while. The fighting at the second wall lasted three days; on the fourth day, unable to withstand Roman valour, they fled within the third wall.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.14.3] Caesar ordered them to refrain from an assault for the moment and commanded only that the second wall be overthrown. Since the greatest part of the war remained, he determined that the soldiers should bring in food for themselves, lest want press upon the victors and scarcity afflict them. For four days the army brought in grain. At the same time, this seemed a suitable interval in which the Jews might take thought for themselves and change their course. The people indeed preferred this, but the leaders of the sedition reckoned up the grievous crimes they had committed against the common people. Hoping for no possibility of pardon, they considered it easier to perish with everyone than to perish alone as the authors of those crimes.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.14.4] On the fifth day, therefore, since no peaceful proposal was brought by the Jews, Caesar attacked the walls in two columns and ordered two siege banks to be raised, one against Antonia and the other against the wall around John’s tomb. With the latter he sought the destruction of the upper city; with the other, if he captured the stronghold, he would easily gain possession of the temple as well. Unless he brought the temple under his control, he could not hold even the city without danger. Titus had divided the army into two bodies. On the opposing side, John and Simon had likewise divided the duties of defence between them. John defended Antonia; Simon, with his armed men and the Idumaean people, kept watch at John’s tomb and from his higher position frustrated all the besiegers’ attempts by whatever means he could. Taught by their sufferings, they were also more practised at countering the siege engines, and had themselves acquired several kinds of engines with which to destroy the Roman works and obstruct their undertakings.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.14.5] Observing their headlong obstinacy, Caesar wished to mingle speech with the siege works, lest despair of pardon make them resist more stubbornly, while hope of what was promised might induce them to desist. He therefore began to urge them not to involve themselves in the destruction of the captured city, but to yield it to his power, since it was already held by arms and, encircled by the siege, was being pressed towards utter ruin. He would grant pardon to those who yielded, if only they took thought either for themselves or for their fatherland, so that the whole city should not be demolished. He also instructed Josephus to address the citizens himself in their native language, in the hope that he might at least bend his fellow tribesmen to renounce their own fury. Although Josephus knew the Jews’ unrestrained hatred towards him, he nevertheless stood as far from the walls as he could with regard to an arrow’s range, yet so that he could be heard, and expounded what would benefit the citizens in the language familiar to him.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.15.1] “It may have been human nature, Hebrews, to persist obstinately before matters came to the final crisis, while you thought that your position and the resources of a familiar region would give you the advantage. Admittedly, it was fitting not to provoke with arms the Romans, invincible in war, who had often defeated those who defeated you; yet thoughtless human minds do fall into this error in prosperity. Moreover, the outcome of war is often uncertain, and so everyone entrusts himself to fortune even when inferior in valour. Finally, you placed your hopes in the walls; you did not think that matters would go so far as the overthrow of the temple. Spare the altars, spare the sacrificial altars, spare the dwelling once heavenly. For now God himself too has abandoned you, because you have abandoned the practice of devotion. We have endured war in the midst of the temple. Fires spread around and range over the temple, but the armed men surrounding it are not such as used to be there. Yet, with hands still free of sacrilege, they wish to spare it, neither to defile its sacred doorposts nor to abolish its ancient rites, if you permit them. What further is awaited? Two walls have been overthrown; the third remains, itself weaker than the two that have fallen. Or is divine protection hoped for, and help from the inner sanctuary? But he who defended us has gone over to the enemy, since the Romans revere him whom we worshipped, while we offend him. Who does not know that God is with those who have subjected everything to themselves except what excessive heat or frost makes inaccessible, and which therefore lies outside Roman dominion because it also lies beyond human use? No one denies that God has given power to different peoples in turn, first to the Egyptians, then to the Jews, and that he has also been a helper to the Assyrians and Persians; afterwards he turned to the Romans and remains with them. Indeed, all kingdoms have yielded to them, and the whole earth has been given into their possession. What have you to do with the conquerors of the whole earth, to whom the secrets of the ocean and the furthest reaches of India lie open? Why should I add the Britains, divided from the whole world by the intervening sea, but brought by the Romans into the inhabited world? Scothia, which owes nothing to the mainland, trembles before them; so does Saxonia, inaccessible through its marshes and enclosed by impassable regions. Although it seems to dare the stealthy raids of war, it too has often figured as a captive in Roman triumphs. It is said to be a very strong race of men, surpassing the rest, yet it relies on pirate skiffs, not on strength, prepared for flight rather than war. But you reply that it is better to die than to lose freedom. When has this judgement succeeded for you, Jews, or when among the Hebrews has useful slavery not been preferred to useless freedom? The patriarch Jacob himself led the Hebrews down into Egypt, lest they perish of hunger. The patriarchs, his twelve sons, went down together, those illustrious beginnings of our race. There was that noble Judah, the stock of the Jews, who gave his name to the people. There Joseph, exalted in chariot and horses, preferred to submit to another’s power so that he might feed his own people, rather than return to the freedom of his own origin. There Benjamin, detained by his brother’s loving deception, consented to the trick, because it was no crime to serve those more powerful. There their descendants, though called away by Moses, nevertheless desired to remain. Thus even harsh slavery was not so displeasing to your fathers that they could not prefer it to dangers. You served the Egyptians, then, and would that it had been only once! Yet you served not only then, when you preferred the food of the harshest slavery to showers of heavenly food, but also afterwards, when you went down into Egypt defeated and captive as you fled the Assyrians. You served the Macedonians too; you served the Assyrians too for many courses of years, and that slavery was sweet. You served Persians, Seleucians and Palestinians; only the Romans do you think burdensome, though those whom you served also serve them. Do you therefore owe hatred or gratitude to those who have made you equal to your masters? I consider this vengeance on your behalf, not an insult, because they have avenged you upon those to whom you were subject. The Assyrian who ruled all Asia is oppressed by servitude. The Egyptian ploughs for the Romans; he sows from his own resources what he is to reap for them. Macedonia, which had conquered Persia and extended its dominion as far as the Indians, acknowledges masters it did not know, and recalls in vain that it gave its kings the name of Aeacids, and that it yielded only to a Roman triumph. Even Pyrrhus himself, displaying both the lineage and the name of Achilles’ stock, was defeated by their arms and submitted so completely in his zeal to obtain peace that he begged for pardon. For why should I speak of the Palestinians, whom the authority of a single governor restrains? Ungrateful men, is it not an honour for you to serve alongside the Persians? For this is to serve alongside kingdoms and to have kings as the greatest consolation in subjection. But I ask when you were free, you who now refuse slavery. When, then, were you free? Even when you ruled others, were you not under a king? You had God as king; you rejected the rule of him under whom alone you were free. You wished to serve men. Why do you tear up your fathers’ testaments, you inheritance rebellious even against your fathers? You chose a king named Saul. When he was killed, the Palestinian people ruled you. After a time David succeeded to the kingship of the whole people, a gentler master indeed, but a master nevertheless. Before he rested, David too imposed a king upon the nation. From Solomon onwards the kingdom was again split in two, and the inheritance of rule divided through a long succession. To pass over the captivities, Cyrus restored many Jews to their lands and their sacred rites. But your fathers, when worn down by grievous battles with the Persians, though illustrious through the triumphs of the Maccabees, chose alliance with Rome. Divine Scripture preserves the agreements of many embassies. You became friends of the Romans, you who had been slaves of the Persians. But again you preferred to have a king rather than a chief priest whom the people should obey. When the cruelty of your kings became intolerable, with Herod dead and Archelaus expelled, you asked to be under the Roman Caesar. You handed yourselves over to Caesar, to whom all are subject, so as to exchange your servitude for a milder one. For to serve in a condition common to everyone is a kind of freedom, since the dignity of the rulers lends honour to the obedience of slaves. Yet the Romans do not exact slavery, being founders of freedom: they not only killed a cruel king but would not tolerate even a proud one. Thus the name of imperial rule is august among them because it increases the prosperity of its own people, not because it oppresses foreigners. But let it be so: let it be useful for you not to obey Roman rule. Let us see whether it is open to you, whether it is not fatal. The Roman battle lines press upon you, the ruins of your country press upon you, the destruction of the temple will press upon you. Weigh not what is useful but what is possible. For it is not the form of your wishes but the reckoning of what is possible that must be weighed. The same law of nature has surely been implanted in all—in men, birds, wild animals and beasts—that each should yield to the more powerful: the bull to the lion, the stag to the bear, the roe deer to the leopard, the hawk to the eagle, the dove to the hawk, and, lest there seem to be some difference arising from diversity of kind, weaker young bulls to the bull himself, flocks of sheep to the ram, goats to the he-goat, and you to those stronger than yourselves. And now what else does Caesar strive for but that your land should not be deserted, your region not emptied, your city not overthrown, your temple not burnt? Victory is not given to all. Nature has given it to a few to rule, to the many to obey. Bulls stand above herds, rams above flocks. Pre-eminence belongs to the few, meekness to the many. You too must put on meekness; accept the subjection that even wild animals put on.” As Josephus said these things, they hurled insults from the wall and cursed him for advising what was useful. But since he could not bend their untamed spirits by reason, he thought that they must also be confronted with the testimonies of Scripture, especially because they said that God would not fail to protect his temple.
paragraphs.runningText: “It may have been human nature, Hebrews, to persist obstinately before matters came to the final crisis, while you thought that your position and the resources of a familiar region would give you the advantage. Admittedly, it was fitting not to provoke with arms the Romans, invincible in war, who had often defeated those who defeated you; yet thoughtless human minds do fall into this error in prosperity. Moreover, the outcome of war is often uncertain, and so everyone entrusts himself to fortune even when inferior in valour. Finally, you placed your hopes in the walls; you did not think that matters would go so far as the overthrow of the temple. Spare the altars, spare the sacrificial altars, spare the dwelling once heavenly. For now God himself too has abandoned you, because you have abandoned the practice of devotion. We have endured war in the midst of the temple. Fires spread around and range over the temple, but the armed men surrounding it are not such as used to be there. Yet, with hands still free of sacrilege, they wish to spare it, neither to defile its sacred doorposts nor to abolish its ancient rites, if you permit them. What further is awaited? Two walls have been overthrown; the third remains, itself weaker than the two that have fallen. Or is divine protection hoped for, and help from the inner sanctuary? But he who defended us has gone over to the enemy, since the Romans revere him whom we worshipped, while we offend him. Who does not know that God is with those who have subjected everything to themselves except what excessive heat or frost makes inaccessible, and which therefore lies outside Roman dominion because it also lies beyond human use? No one denies that God has given power to different peoples in turn, first to the Egyptians, then to the Jews, and that he has also been a helper to the Assyrians and Persians; afterwards he turned to the Romans and remains with them. Indeed, all kingdoms have yielded to them, and the whole earth has been given into their possession. What have you to do with the conquerors of the whole earth, to whom the secrets of the ocean and the furthest reaches of India lie open? Why should I add the Britains, divided from the whole world by the intervening sea, but brought by the Romans into the inhabited world? Scothia, which owes nothing to the mainland, trembles before them; so does Saxonia, inaccessible through its marshes and enclosed by impassable regions. Although it seems to dare the stealthy raids of war, it too has often figured as a captive in Roman triumphs. It is said to be a very strong race of men, surpassing the rest, yet it relies on pirate skiffs, not on strength, prepared for flight rather than war. But you reply that it is better to die than to lose freedom. When has this judgement succeeded for you, Jews, or when among the Hebrews has useful slavery not been preferred to useless freedom? The patriarch Jacob himself led the Hebrews down into Egypt, lest they perish of hunger. The patriarchs, his twelve sons, went down together, those illustrious beginnings of our race. There was that noble Judah, the stock of the Jews, who gave his name to the people. There Joseph, exalted in chariot and horses, preferred to submit to another’s power so that he might feed his own people, rather than return to the freedom of his own origin. There Benjamin, detained by his brother’s loving deception, consented to the trick, because it was no crime to serve those more powerful. There their descendants, though called away by Moses, nevertheless desired to remain. Thus even harsh slavery was not so displeasing to your fathers that they could not prefer it to dangers. You served the Egyptians, then, and would that it had been only once! Yet you served not only then, when you preferred the food of the harshest slavery to showers of heavenly food, but also afterwards, when you went down into Egypt defeated and captive as you fled the Assyrians. You served the Macedonians too; you served the Assyrians too for many courses of years, and that slavery was sweet. You served Persians, Seleucians and Palestinians; only the Romans do you think burdensome, though those whom you served also serve them. Do you therefore owe hatred or gratitude to those who have made you equal to your masters? I consider this vengeance on your behalf, not an insult, because they have avenged you upon those to whom you were subject. The Assyrian who ruled all Asia is oppressed by servitude.
