paragraphs.rawText: [V.16.1] “Rash men, do you hope that divine help will come to you only now, when you have thrown everything into confusion with arms, violated the altars with war and torn down the defences of the whole city? Rash men,” he said, “forgetful of your own sources of help, have you prepared shields and swords, and these against the Romans? You were not accustomed to conquer with such arms. For when did the Hebrews’ victory lie in spear and sword? Remember whence you arose and from whom you came, how your fathers conquered their enemies. Rash men, what a helper you have taken from yourselves while demanding help from elsewhere! Father Abraham entered Egypt not with a multitude of people but in the fear of God. When he saw the chastity of his abducted wife held captive, he nevertheless abstained from war, took up the arms of devout prayer and called in a defender to overcome the sleeping king and, with the enemy defeated, restore his wife to him undefiled. Sarah returned without arms, bringing her husband a triumphal victory. Abraham slept and Pharaoh was tormented. Sarah feared and Pharaoh denied the crime; he sent away another man’s wife and, condemning the crime, honoured the chastity he had desired to despoil. He added gold and silver in honour of Sarah’s modesty, to condemn an intention that had not issued in a crime. He begged father Abraham to pray to the Lord for his household, for his house was barren. Sarah came back richer, with her modesty intact; Abraham returned holier, having repaid the reward for his wife’s chastity with a remedy for barrenness. What shall I say of his son Isaac? He too relied on the protection his father had enjoyed and did not bring out armed battle lines against the insolence of a powerful neighbour. Yet he certainly had a strong band of three hundred and eighteen men born in his household, who had defeated five kings in war, stripped them of their spoils and restored the captive Lot to his uncle Abraham. He did not draw his sword from its sheath, but clothed himself only in patience against those who envied him and answered them with guilelessness. Those who had declared that he must be driven out came to entreat him; those who could not bear him as a neighbour sought his friendship. I tremble to recount such great wonders of the fathers. Holy Jacob, when his brother Esau threatened the murder of his own kin, left his country and abandoned his parents, carrying with him prayer alone as provision for the journey. Deservedly, while in foreign places he feared his brother’s ambushes and lacked the company and help of men, he found an assembly of angels. Brought, as he says, to the Camp of God, he wrestled with the Lord and, as Scripture says, prevailed against God, though he thought himself no match for men. What else did Moses raise against the king of the Egyptians, his army and his serpents but his rod alone? O powerful rod, which covered heaven with darkness, flooded the earth with rain and dried the sea of its waves! The Egyptians had surrounded the Hebrews; Moses prayed and did not fight. The sea was divided and the people entered; Pharaoh followed, and Moses, placed amid the waves, prayed. Pharaoh was drowned with his men; Moses sang. Who, considering so many and such great things, would not marvel and understand that our arms are better in prayer than in valour? For prayer calls divine help to itself, valour the help of the body. These arms, which are not carnal but mighty through God, were learnt by Moses’ disciple and successor, Joshua son of Nun. An imitator and near equal of his master, he turned the waters of the Jordan backwards; and when he saw the impregnable walls of the city of Jericho, he ordered the priests to sound the trumpet and the people to shout. When this was done, the walls suddenly fell, the city was burnt and all were killed except those whom the faith of Rahab, the good prostitute, protected from the destruction of that city. Gideon too chose three hundred men for war, and commanded them to carry before them mysteries, not arms: in the left hand jars full of water, in the right torches. Struck by this sight, the enemy fled at once, and victory came to the Hebrews. Care for sacred religion had been neglected through the negligence of Eli the priest; the divine commands were being abandoned. Foreigners brought war upon them, the Hebrews were defeated, and even the ark of God was captured. Yet it was returned without any arms. By this sign it became clear both that arms do not conquer without religion and that religion conquers without arms. When the Assyrian people poured into the Jewish nation, King Hezekiah learnt fully what insults were hurled at God through the voice of Rabshakeh at King Sennacherib’s command, and what utter destruction was threatened against the people. On receiving the report, he did not think that words must be answered with words or arms with arms. Rising, he clothed himself in sackcloth as in a shield, covered his head with ashes instead of a helmet and hurled prayer instead of javelins. Prayer ascended; an angel descended. During the night one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians were slain. We counted the corpses; we did not see the slayer. I had passed over the five kings who began a war without consulting the Lord. As they travelled through the desert, lack of water began to afflict them severely, and thirst tormented both them and their horses. Necessity compelled them to make good the duty they had neglected. For the king of Israel was negligent in the worship of God, but, urged by the others to seek out the Lord’s prophet, he learnt that Elisha was not far from the very places where they were staying. They sent to beg the help of his prayer and remedies for their need. Although he was offended with the king of Israel because the faithless man did not believe, he nevertheless promised both an abundance of water and a speedy victory. Water began to flow through the desert, and streams poured of their own accord over the land without any rain. The adversaries rose, having been sunk in a deeper sleep, their anxiety relaxed by their confidence of victory. Suddenly they saw the waters turn red as the sun poured upon them, and thought that a battle had been fought among the kings’ peoples, with whose blood the earth was wet. So, hurrying for plunder, they ran everywhere without order or restraint, each trying to get ahead of the other. Having rushed headlong into the midst of the enemy, they were surrounded and killed, and a great slaughter was made of them. Thus the holy prophet drove both thirst and fear from our fathers. The same man also brought help against famine. For when Samaria was besieged and the king of Israel remained shut within it, grievous hunger pressed upon them, so that they did not abstain even from abominable food. Confronted by the hideousness of so great a misery and by the messenger of the king, who thought that the famine had grown through the prophet’s neglect, he answered: ‘On the following day you will see both an abundance of grain and a low price.’ He told the messenger who did not believe that he himself, because he did not believe, would not see it, but that the promises would nevertheless be fulfilled. Suddenly during the night the neighing of horses, the crash of chariots, the roar of four-horse chariots running and the sound of arms were heard in the Syrian camp and struck fear into the victors: many strong nations had come, they thought, to help the Hebrews. They hastened to escape by flight the danger which they believed was imminent. Night hastened their decision and increased their terror. So, after the Syrians fled, all the supplies they had seized were found in the camp the following day. Abundance created low prices; low prices fulfilled the promise; the death of the unbeliever deprived him of its fruit, but did not prevent the remedy for all. It is clear, then, that many leaders among our fathers attained victory when they did not fight at all, and that others too prevailed in war when, after they sought counsel, an oracle permitted them to fight. Thus Amalek was defeated, but when Moses raised his hands; Joshua son of Nun conquered when he made the sun stand still; Gideon conquered when he had tested at the water those who were to fight; Samson too, while he still kept his hair undefiled; and Samuel conquered, but when he had resolved to set up a helper stone. David triumphed when, in prophetic mysteries, he had joined Bathsheba, that is, the daughter of the Sabbath, to himself in marriage. He conquered in civil war too, which he fled when it was brought upon him, and did not himself bring about. For nothing is fouler than civil war except only the man who could bring it about. Asaph too conquered in battle, but only after he said to his men, who despaired because they were inferior in number, that it made no difference whether they were few or many, since God makes a few who fear him stronger than the many. He was truly good in faith, if only he had persevered to the end. A woman too conquered by arms, having kept faith with God. Saul, however, was defeated because he did not keep God’s commands. Josiah was wounded because he advanced against the enemy contrary to command; otherwise holy, he was therefore snatched away so that he might not see the captivity due to our sins. Necho cried out, ‘I have not been sent against you’, bearing witness to his faith; but participation in a degenerate alliance ensnared him, as it had Amaziah before him. Amaziah had in fact been warned by a man of God to dismiss those whom he had hired as allies in war for a hundred talents of silver, if he wished to conquer. When he hesitated because he would lose so great a payment, the prophet answered that the Lord had more from which to restore even the silver to him. Relying on this, he dismissed the hired auxiliaries and conquered with fewer men. Yet he too failed to pay God the reward for so great a victory, but immediately offered sacrifices to the very images he had captured as victor, as though he had conquered through the favour of those he had reduced to captive booty. Zedekiah himself, with the ruin of his country already upon him, was warned through the prophet Jeremiah, while pressed by the enemy’s siege, not to fear leaving the city: he would be victorious if he obeyed the heavenly commands, or a captive if he thought it must be defended. Through faithlessness he deceived himself and his own people. The Jewish people had been carried away by the Assyrians into Babylonia; the rest, who had remained, were deliberating about moving to the Egyptians. The Lord commanded through the prophet Isaiah and the others that they should be content with the rule of one nation, lest a double captivity increase their hardship. But they disregarded God’s oracles and became captives of two nations, having impatiently desired to escape the yoke of one. Thus they remained exiles in Egypt. Those who had been led away among the Assyrians, however, after the time of captivity which the Lord had appointed for the people’s sins was fulfilled, later obtained permission to go back under Cyrus’s rule and returned with favour. God’s temple was renewed with the resources of Kings Cyrus and Darius and the gifts of the other Persians. Thus the very men who had overthrown it provided the cost of its repair; they also restored the rights of the priests and assisted the practice of religion. Our own people, however, while competing with one another for the priesthood and courting the Parthians to have that honour conferred upon them, made merchandise of religion. Why do we complain of the Babylonians? We have found our own people worse. Those men restored to us the right of religious observance, those men restored the appointment of priests, and our own people handed it back to the Persians. Those men left the priestly fillets in our power; our own people made them tributary to the Babylonians. Why should I add that the sanctuary is stained with blood, that the sacred thresholds drip with blood, that the temple’s gables still stand half ruined? God’s anger towards us is less than our own strife. His anger made us captives; our strife made us sacrilegious. His anger scattered the Jews; our strife destroyed them. Compare, if you please, the difference between our captivity and our sedition: our captivity brought the gentiles a share in our religion, while our sedition deprived even the Jews of the grace of religion. Who brought the Romans into Judaea but the strife of Hyrcanus and Aristobulus? Who brought Sossius but Herod? Who brought Antony but Sossius? Who begged Caesar to be their king but you? Who other than you expelled Antipater from the kingdom, and freedom in Antipater? Yet I do not reproach you, nor do I deny that Florus acted criminally against you. But a complaint should have been brought to the Romans, not war. You despised Nero. But Vespasian had succeeded him, kindly by nature, yet capable of being still kinder from inclination, because he had assumed imperial rule in Judaea. Or, if his compassion did not move you, his valour certainly ought to have driven you to take thought for yourselves. But how would he not spare you, when he spared Josephus? For to whom ought he to have been more hostile than to me? Who built greater defences against the Romans? Who thought more zealously that the contest must be fought for our country, once you had chosen war? I did not approve the beginnings of wars, but once they were undertaken I did not abandon them. The ashes of the city of Jotapata, which sheltered me while I was still fighting, bear witness to this: that I did not desist from war until after that city’s ruin; that I lay hidden as long as I could in that tomb of the overthrown city; that I preferred hunger rather than surrender myself to the Romans; that I sought ways of escape to come to you, but was caught and did not come out of my own accord; that I preferred to perish with my own people, but Caesar spared me; that I wished rather to share your danger, not because I approved your counsel, but because I chose to share the danger with you. Yet I thank God that I did not fall into partnership in so great a crime, so that I should not be thought an inciter of seditions or, since I could not join in them, complete through my own death the murder of kin that I could avoid committing with my own hand; certainly, so that I should not see my most holy mother torn apart on my account and the entrails of my own people scattered. These things are indeed pitiable, yet it is more bearable to suffer them than to have done them. What, then, are you still waiting for? The signs of our ancestors? Our merits are not such, nor are our services in the worship of God. The Romans’ faithlessness is not that of the Assyrians, who accepted payment for withdrawal and broke faith, deciding not to retreat but to press on more fiercely. Indeed, to infer the movement of the divine judgement from events, it is certain that God opposes the Jews. Thus Siloam, which had dried up before the war, and all the veins of springs outside the city, which had long ceased to flow so that water was unavailable for our use unless bought at a price, now return to their functions and pour themselves out at Titus’s arrival. Rich veins gush forth, and everything is so filled with overflowing waters that they abound generously not only for the army to drink, but also for war-horses, beasts of burden and all the livestock. Nor is there any lack of abundant water to irrigate the gardens, so that you would think fuller streams were being poured out as though the elements were striving for Roman victory. We recognise the former portents, which then too preceded the capture of our city: water ceased for the Jews and poured forth for the enemy, lest thirst hinder the siege. Nor is it surprising if divine grace has withdrawn from the Jews, whom such great crimes have hemmed in. A good man shuns a lodging full of horror and leaves his own house if he learns that some crime has been committed in it; he avoids sharing an unworthy dwelling and curses the wickedness of those living there. Do we then doubt, concerning the supreme and immaculate God, that he abhors the contagion of so many crimes, turns away from the atrocity of deadly wickedness and does not linger in the assemblies of murderers of kin? He commanded Dathan and Abiram to be separated from the innocent because they had challenged Moses and Aaron by usurping the priestly office, lest a stain contaminate the devout through association with the guilty, or punishment engulf them. But why do I linger longer in words, when scenes full of horror and groaning surround us and the destruction of the temple is being hastened? What eyes can watch this, what senses endure it, what spirit bear it? O men harder than rocks, more unyielding than iron, who amid such monstrous human events still compete with one another in crime as though in emulation of valour! And, what is graver, you yourselves destroy your country and increase its ruins. Turn back at last, come to your senses at last, judge and see the beauty of the country you have betrayed. What a city, what a temple, what dwellings of the saints and inner sanctuaries of sacred rites, what works of the prophets are being disembowelled by your hands! Can anyone direct flames against these, scatter fires and feed conflagrations, and be moved by no feeling? The hardness of rocks, if it could feel, would dissolve. Indeed, even things without feeling often imitate the appearance of feeling in the greatest bitterness of events, so that crags tremble and drops flow as blood moistens them. Yet you remain unmoved: what better thing can remain after these, what more worthy thing have you to preserve? Finally, if these things do not move you, though they are of greater worth among the devout, at least pity your own kindred. Set before your eyes your children’s deaths by the sword or their more bitter deaths by hunger, and the slavery of your wives and daughters. They will have secure freedom through an agreement to surrender, or captive servitude through the city’s overthrow. Take thought while you can, lest you leave behind after your death things more grievous than you have done before death. Nor am I free from danger of this kind. I too know that, together with yours, my mother, most holy to me, and my dear wife are in danger, a lineage by no means ignoble and a house once illustrious. And perhaps you think that I urge these things for the sake of my own people. Kill them, and take my blood besides as payment. Gladly do I pay this price for your safety, if after me you can come to your senses.”

O powerful rod, which covered heaven with darkness, flooded the earth with rain and dried the sea of its waves! The Egyptians had surrounded the Hebrews; Moses prayed and did not fight. The sea was divided and the people entered; Pharaoh followed, and Moses, placed amid the waves, prayed. Pharaoh was drowned with his men; Moses sang. Who, considering so many and such great things, would not marvel and understand that our arms are better in prayer than in valour? For prayer calls divine help to itself, valour the help of the body. These arms, which are not carnal but mighty through God, were learnt by Moses’ disciple and successor, Joshua son of Nun. An imitator and near equal of his master, he turned the waters of the Jordan backwards; and when he saw the impregnable walls of the city of Jericho, he ordered the priests to sound the trumpet and the people to shout. When this was done, the walls suddenly fell, the city was burnt and all were killed except those whom the faith of Rahab, the good prostitute, protected from the destruction of that city. Gideon too chose three hundred men for war, and commanded them to carry before them mysteries, not arms: in the left hand jars full of water, in the right torches. Struck by this sight, the enemy fled at once, and victory came to the Hebrews. Care for sacred religion had been neglected through the negligence of Eli the priest; the divine commands were being abandoned. Foreigners brought war upon them, the Hebrews were defeated, and even the ark of God was captured. Yet it was returned without any arms. By this sign it became clear both that arms do not conquer without religion and that religion conquers without arms. When the Assyrian people poured into the Jewish nation, King Hezekiah learnt fully what insults were hurled at God through the voice of Rabshakeh at King Sennacherib’s command, and what utter destruction was threatened against the people. On receiving the report, he did not think that words must be answered with words or arms with arms. Rising, he clothed himself in sackcloth as in a shield, covered his head with ashes instead of a helmet and hurled prayer instead of javelins. Prayer ascended; an angel descended. During the night one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians were slain. We counted the corpses; we did not see the slayer. I had passed over the five kings who began a war without consulting the Lord. As they travelled through the desert, lack of water began to afflict them severely, and thirst tormented both them and their horses. Necessity compelled them to make good the duty they had neglected. For the king of Israel was negligent in the worship of God, but, urged by the others to seek out the Lord’s prophet, he learnt that Elisha was not far from the very places where they were staying. They sent to beg the help of his prayer and remedies for their need. Although he was offended with the king of Israel because the faithless man did not believe, he nevertheless promised both an abundance of water and a speedy victory. Water began to flow through the desert, and streams poured of their own accord over the land without any rain. The adversaries rose, having been sunk in a deeper sleep, their anxiety relaxed by their confidence of victory. Suddenly they saw the waters turn red as the sun poured upon them, and thought that a battle had been fought among the kings’ peoples, with whose blood the earth was wet. So, hurrying for plunder, they ran everywhere without order or restraint, each trying to get ahead of the other. Having rushed headlong into the midst of the enemy, they were surrounded and killed, and a great slaughter was made of them. Thus the holy prophet drove both thirst and fear from our fathers. The same man also brought help against famine. For when Samaria was besieged and the king of Israel remained shut within it, grievous hunger pressed upon them, so that they did not abstain even from abominable food. Confronted by the hideousness of so great a misery and by the messenger of the king, who thought that the famine had grown through the prophet’s neglect, he answered: ‘On the following day you will see both an abundance of grain and a low price.’ He told the messenger who did not believe that he himself, because he did not believe, would not see it, but that the promises would nevertheless be fulfilled. Suddenly during the night the neighing of horses, the crash of chariots, the roar of four-horse chariots running and the sound of arms were heard in the Syrian camp and struck fear into the victors: many strong nations had come, they thought, to help the Hebrews. They hastened to escape by flight the danger which they believed was imminent. Night hastened their decision and increased their terror. So, after the Syrians fled, all the supplies they had seized were found in the camp the following day. Abundance created low prices; low prices fulfilled the promise; the death of the unbeliever deprived him of its fruit, but did not prevent the remedy for all. It is clear, then, that many leaders among our fathers attained victory when they did not fight at all, and that others too prevailed in war when, after they sought counsel, an oracle permitted them to fight. Thus Amalek was defeated, but when Moses raised his hands; Joshua son of Nun conquered when he made the sun stand still; Gideon conquered when he had tested at the water those who were to fight; Samson too, while he still kept his hair undefiled; and Samuel conquered, but when he had resolved to set up a helper stone. David triumphed when, in prophetic mysteries, he had joined Bathsheba, that is, the daughter of the Sabbath, to himself in marriage. He conquered in civil war too, which he fled when it was brought upon him, and did not himself bring about. For nothing is fouler than civil war except only the man who could bring it about. Asaph too conquered in battle, but only after he said to his men, who despaired because they were inferior in number, that it made no difference whether they were few or many, since God makes a few who fear him stronger than the many. He was truly good in faith, if only he had persevered to the end. A woman too conquered by arms, having kept faith with God. Saul, however, was defeated because he did not keep God’s commands. Josiah was wounded because he advanced against the enemy contrary to command; otherwise holy, he was therefore snatched away so that he might not see the captivity due to our sins. Necho cried out, ‘I have not been sent against you’, bearing witness to his faith; but participation in a degenerate alliance ensnared him, as it had Amaziah before him. Amaziah had in fact been warned by a man of God to dismiss those whom he had hired as allies in war for a hundred talents of silver, if he wished to conquer. When he hesitated because he would lose so great a payment, the prophet answered that the Lord had more from which to restore even the silver to him. Relying on this, he dismissed the hired auxiliaries and conquered with fewer men. Yet he too failed to pay God the reward for so great a victory, but immediately offered sacrifices to the very images he had captured as victor, as though he had conquered through the favour of those he had reduced to captive booty. Zedekiah himself, with the ruin of his country already upon him, was warned through the prophet Jeremiah, while pressed by the enemy’s siege, not to fear leaving the city: he would be victorious if he obeyed the heavenly commands, or a captive if he thought it must be defended. Through faithlessness he deceived himself and his own people. The Jewish people had been carried away by the Assyrians into Babylonia; the rest, who had remained, were deliberating about moving to the Egyptians. The Lord commanded through the prophet Isaiah and the others that they should be content with the rule of one nation, lest a double captivity increase their hardship. But they disregarded God’s oracles and became captives of two nations, having impatiently desired to escape the yoke of one. Thus they remained exiles in Egypt. Those who had been led away among the Assyrians, however, after the time of captivity which the Lord had appointed for the people’s sins was fulfilled, later obtained permission to go back under Cyrus’s rule and returned with favour. God’s temple was renewed with the resources of Kings Cyrus and Darius and the gifts of the other Persians. Thus the very men who had overthrown it provided the cost of its repair; they also restored the rights of the priests and assisted the practice of religion. Our own people, however, while competing with one another for the priesthood and courting the Parthians to have that honour conferred upon them, made merchandise of religion. Why do we complain of the Babylonians? We have found our own people worse. Those men restored to us the right of religious observance, those men restored the appointment of priests, and our own people handed it back to the Persians. Those men left the priestly fillets in our power; our own people made them tributary to the Babylonians. Why should I add that the sanctuary is stained with blood, that the sacred thresholds drip with blood, that the temple’s gables still stand half ruined? God’s anger towards us is less than our own strife. His anger made us captives; our strife made us sacrilegious. His anger scattered the Jews; our strife destroyed them. Compare, if you please, the difference between our captivity and our sedition: our captivity brought the gentiles a share in our religion, while our sedition deprived even the Jews of the grace of religion. Who brought the Romans into Judaea but the strife of Hyrcanus and Aristobulus? Who brought Sossius but Herod? Who brought Antony but Sossius? Who begged Caesar to be their king but you? Who other than you expelled Antipater from the kingdom, and freedom in Antipater? Yet I do not reproach you, nor do I deny that Florus acted criminally against you. But a complaint should have been brought to the Romans, not war. You despised Nero. But Vespasian had succeeded him, kindly by nature, yet capable of being still kinder from inclination, because he had assumed imperial rule in Judaea. Or, if his compassion did not move you, his valour certainly ought to have driven you to take thought for yourselves. But how would he not spare you, when he spared Josephus? For to whom ought he to have been more hostile than to me? Who built greater defences against the Romans? Who thought more zealously that the contest must be fought for our country, once you had chosen war? I did not approve the beginnings of wars, but once they were undertaken I did not abandon them. The ashes of the city of Jotapata, which sheltered me while I was still fighting, bear witness to this: that I did not desist from war until after that city’s ruin; that I lay hidden as long as I could in that tomb of the overthrown city; that I preferred hunger rather than surrender myself to the Romans; that I sought ways of escape to come to you, but was caught and did not come out of my own accord; that I preferred to perish with my own people, but Caesar spared me; that I wished rather to share your danger, not because I approved your counsel, but because I chose to share the danger with you. Yet I thank God that I did not fall into partnership in so great a crime, so that I should not be thought an inciter of seditions or, since I could not join in them, complete through my own death the murder of kin that I could avoid committing with my own hand; certainly, so that I should not see my most holy mother torn apart on my account and the entrails of my own people scattered. These things are indeed pitiable, yet it is more bearable to suffer them than to have done them. What, then, are you still waiting for? The signs of our ancestors? Our merits are not such, nor are our services in the worship of God. The Romans’ faithlessness is not that of the Assyrians, who accepted payment for withdrawal and broke faith, deciding not to retreat but to press on more fiercely. Indeed, to infer the movement of the divine judgement from events, it is certain that God opposes the Jews. Thus Siloam, which had dried up before the war, and all the veins of springs outside the city, which had long ceased to flow so that water was unavailable for our use unless bought at a price, now return to their functions and pour themselves out at Titus’s arrival. Rich veins gush forth, and everything is so filled with overflowing waters that they abound generously not only for the army to drink, but also for war-horses, beasts of burden and all the livestock. Nor is there any lack of abundant water to irrigate the gardens, so that you would think fuller streams were being poured out as though the elements were striving for Roman victory. We recognise the former portents, which then too preceded the capture of our city: water ceased for the Jews and poured forth for the enemy, lest thirst hinder the siege. Nor is it surprising if divine grace has withdrawn from the Jews, whom such great crimes have hemmed in. A good man shuns a lodging full of horror and leaves his own house if he learns that some crime has been committed in it; he avoids sharing an unworthy dwelling and curses the wickedness of those living there. Do we then doubt, concerning the supreme and immaculate God, that he abhors the contagion of so many crimes, turns away from the atrocity of deadly wickedness and does not linger in the assemblies of murderers of kin? He commanded Dathan and Abiram to be separated from the innocent because they had challenged Moses and Aaron by usurping the priestly office, lest a stain contaminate the devout through association with the guilty, or punishment engulf them. But why do I linger longer in words, when scenes full of horror and groaning surround us and the destruction of the temple is being hastened? What eyes can watch this, what senses endure it, what spirit bear it? O men harder than rocks, more unyielding than iron, who amid such monstrous human events still compete with one another in crime as though in emulation of valour! And, what is graver, you yourselves destroy your country and increase its ruins. Turn back at last, come to your senses at last, judge and see the beauty of the country you have betrayed. What a city, what a temple, what dwellings of the saints and inner sanctuaries of sacred rites, what works of the prophets are being disembowelled by your hands! Can anyone direct flames against these, scatter fires and feed conflagrations, and be moved by no feeling? The hardness of rocks, if it could feel, would dissolve. Indeed, even things without feeling often imitate the appearance of feeling in the greatest bitterness of events, so that crags tremble and drops flow as blood moistens them. Yet you remain unmoved: what better thing can remain after these, what more worthy thing have you to preserve? Finally, if these things do not move you, though they are of greater worth among the devout, at least pity your own kindred. Set before your eyes your children’s deaths by the sword or their more bitter deaths by hunger, and the slavery of your wives and daughters. They will have secure freedom through an agreement to surrender, or captive servitude through the city’s overthrow. Take thought while you can, lest you leave behind after your death things more grievous than you have done before death. Nor am I free from danger of this kind. I too know that, together with yours, my mother, most holy to me, and my dear wife are in danger, a lineage by no means ignoble and a house once illustrious. And perhaps you think that I urge these things for the sake of my own people. Kill them, and take my blood besides as payment. Gladly do I pay this price for your safety, if after me you can come to your senses.”

paragraphs.rawText: [V.17.1] Josephus cried out these things with tears and moved many of the people to take refuge with the Romans after selling what they possessed. Titus sent each of them where he wished to go, so that the others too might be encouraged to surrender themselves to the Romans without fear. Thus, when they found an opportunity to leave, they streamed out, assured of safety if they reached the Romans and unconcerned about slavery, since their freedom was preserved. But those who followed John and Simon, the arbiters and inciters of sedition, feared punishment for their crimes more than the adversities of war, and therefore thought that refuge would be unsafe for them. Not only did they themselves not dare to leave, but they also kept watch to prevent anyone of the people from leaving the city, taking greater care to guard against the departure of their own people than the entry of the Romans. Thus people were held against their will, and anyone caught paid a grievous penalty. A slight suspicion was the cause of a most grievous death. Truth was sought not through evidence but through torments. If any were wealthy, they were dragged to death on a fabricated charge of treason; equally, if any were poor, they lay exposed to death because they had nothing with which to redeem themselves.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.18.1] Hunger too had begun to rage, and sedition to run still more rampant in fury and madness. Grain could not be found; no bread was available for public consumption. Wherever it was discovered, the house was immediately stormed. The owner of the house or the person who had stored the grain was slaughtered for having hidden it. Again, if no grain was found, tortures were inflicted as though it had been hidden more carefully. Many wished for the short way out through death, since either hunger afflicted them or cruelty tormented them. Indeed, the more savage men disdained to kill, grudging the benefit of death to those whose more violent executioner, hunger, had already eaten away their flesh in pitiable wasting and covered their bare bones with thin skin. Half dead, with only breath still remaining, they breathed and dragged their sickly corpses along. If they saw vegetable scraps that had fallen by chance or been thrown away as dried up, powerless in the rest of their bodies, they licked with their mouths what lay on the ground. Or if they saw grass growing in the walls, they snatched it and consoled their miserable hunger with its wretched juice. The richer bought a measure of wheat for their entire fortune—for why should they preserve what would be of no use?—and the poorer a measure of barley, taking care that no one saw either seller or buyer, for this was punished more severely than any crime. Nor did they wait for the bread to be baked, lest death forestall them or delay summon an informer. Hidden in secret places, those who had any supply of grain, however small, chewed the wheat uncooked. There was no table, no seat, no light, lest someone come upon them and catch them unawares. At any sound the food was hidden. Solitude was suspect, gatherings murderous towards kin; among their own people there was a grim struggle.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.18.2] For hunger excludes every affection, and above all shame. For the hungry, modesty costs life and diminishes the chance of survival. If a man with a wife, children or grandchildren had any food, he scarcely admitted it. The same was true of the women. But if someone of a gentler spirit set out food, it was wrenched from their hands. The food was pitiable, the meal tearful. Children snatched from parents, parents from children, and food was brought out of their very throats. For many, the vomit of others became food. There was no horror at taking putrid things, no shame at robbing their own people of the last drops of life. Even this spectacle of so wretched a calamity feared discovery. Thus it was enacted behind closed doors, lest someone come upon them seeking food from another’s mouth and, like a dog, lick up another’s vomit with his tongue. Not even this went unpunished, for wherever doors were barred, a deceit involving hidden food was suspected. The agents of sedition rushed forward, stormed what was closed and exacted intolerable torments of a new cruelty. Not even the private parts of the body were spared. Punishment passed through these too, because the sensation of pain is more grievous in them. Many, when they saw the killers already bursting in, snatched up the food they had prepared, so that they themselves might not be cheated of their last provisions, or at least might avenge the death to come. And what made the cruelty seem more grievous was that those who snatched food from the hungry were not themselves hungry. For through plunder they had heaped up the resources of others for themselves and fed on others’ stores, while those who had gathered them wasted away in hunger and fasting. If a mother, stirred by maternal affection and pitying an infant’s cries, wished to pour the juice of food from her own mouth into the child’s, she paid the penalty for a work of devotion: she was pierced together with her child, whether it hung from her neck or clung to her breasts. Many too, thinking death a benefit, went out of the city to pluck herbs, feed on roots or strip bark from trees, in case their green growth supplied anything to console hunger; when the Romans found them, they killed them. Or one who had escaped the enemy collapsed on the very threshold of the gate, wasted by hunger and feeble in the mouth, no longer able even to chew. Those who returned were also met by a more savage band, which wrenched from the folds of the wretches’ garments what they had sought at the greatest peril, committing the bitterest crime and leaving them no share even as a reward for the danger. Thus they died under greater violence from their own people than from the enemy. For what even the enemy had allowed them a fellow citizen snatched away. Yet it was no use to have snatched food of this kind. For not long afterwards, though their bodies were still vigorous, their bellies swelled and they were shaken by pain deep in their entrails, or, their bowels loosened, they failed with their strength exhausted, so that they regretted wishing for what was a consolation for a time and afterwards a torment. Then, with green lizards and the cooked remains of other creatures of the serpent kind, they added pestilence. For if they happened to find the carcasses of horses, they pulled them between themselves and settled the matter in a fierce fight. Nor was there any respite from the destruction heaped upon them by the enemy. For very many left the city with their children and wives and withdrew to the part which curved into the depths of steep ravines. The Romans kept watch, either to lead off captives as slaves, especially the younger ones, or to strike down the stronger, lest anyone dare to steal upon the combatants. Thus, if anyone went further afield in search of food, digging for the roots of wild plants, he was intercepted.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.18.3] Yet even with the enemy surrounding them, they could not restrain themselves, for hunger gave them boldness. Parental affection could not bear to see their little children consumed by wasting, their mouths opened in hunger and stretched out in vain. They had taken the children with them to share the danger, lest the authors of sedition kill them in their place, as hostages for their flight. Hunger compelled them to go out, since death by the sword was a benefit compared with starvation. The Romans, on the other hand, because they thought them contemptuous of death, increased the kinds of torture, first beating them and then fastening to the cross’s gibbet whomever they encountered, so that at least the sight of their torments might recall the others’ rashness from insolent provocation. Thus their suffering and the bitterness of such great calamities seemed pitiable to Titus. Countless people were captured; about five hundred a day were tortured, lining the fields before the city in the order of a pitiable procession, so that they could be seen from the walls. The Romans pitied them, the Jews were unmoved; the enemy shared their suffering, their comrades did not relent; compassion was more readily found among adversaries than among comrades. Yet many of the Romans were inflamed with indignation because the Jews became worse amid such great evils. You could see people fastened in different ways and various kinds of punishment and forms of torment, in such an innumerable multitude that space was now lacking for gibbets, gibbets for bodies. Within, Simon raged and John roared; through their agents they laid traps for individuals. If anyone tried to flee, he was dragged along the ground and torn apart. The relatives of those who had left were also tortured, or the corpses of many, fastened to a cross, were displayed to their own people who had escaped. On the opposite side they too had lined the wall with a kind of crop of gibbets, as though triumphing over adversaries, whenever they caught any of their own people wishing to flee to the Romans, so that fear of desertion might seize the others. No place was free of bitterness: outside captivity, within hunger, fear on both sides. Yet arms were feared less than torments, and it was easier to be killed amid the enemy’s tumult than by the murder of kin. Yet Caesar did not cease to invite the faction leaders to the hope offered by surrender. For, with the siege banks built, he announced that the effect of the work would not be long delayed and that destruction threatened the city: they should take thought for themselves, so that they might gain safety and the temple too might be rescued from the flames. To make them believe this more readily, many Jews were sent with their hands cut off, lest they be thought to have crossed over to the Romans by voluntary desertion and so be denied belief as faithless men, or be killed by their own people. But in return for his continual admonition they hurled back grievous insults. Caesar’s humanity seemed to them more deadly than his cruelty, because the one took away freedom, the other life. They preferred to die free rather than live as slaves. They had devoted their lives to the temple. Immortality would be theirs if, burnt with the temple, they died upon the altars and hearths of their fathers. Titus had accomplished nothing; he had taken away little and given more. Paradise would take the temple’s place for them, and they, who had fought for God’s temple, would be transferred there, provided only that they did not see Roman triumphs with their own eyes or submit captive necks to the yoke. Their little children, whose parents had been champions of the heavenly mysteries, were being consecrated, not killed. Titus, all the more stirred to rescue at least those who were being held against their will, ordered the engines to be brought up.

Within, Simon raged and John roared; through their agents they laid traps for individuals. If anyone tried to flee, he was dragged along the ground and torn apart. The relatives of those who had left were also tortured, or the corpses of many, fastened to a cross, were displayed to their own people who had escaped. On the opposite side they too had lined the wall with a kind of crop of gibbets, as though triumphing over adversaries, whenever they caught any of their own people wishing to flee to the Romans, so that fear of desertion might seize the others. No place was free of bitterness: outside captivity, within hunger, fear on both sides. Yet arms were feared less than torments, and it was easier to be killed amid the enemy’s tumult than by the murder of kin. Yet Caesar did not cease to invite the faction leaders to the hope offered by surrender. For, with the siege banks built, he announced that the effect of the work would not be long delayed and that destruction threatened the city: they should take thought for themselves, so that they might gain safety and the temple too might be rescued from the flames. To make them believe this more readily, many Jews were sent with their hands cut off, lest they be thought to have crossed over to the Romans by voluntary desertion and so be denied belief as faithless men, or be killed by their own people. But in return for his continual admonition they hurled back grievous insults. Caesar’s humanity seemed to them more deadly than his cruelty, because the one took away freedom, the other life. They preferred to die free rather than live as slaves. They had devoted their lives to the temple. Immortality would be theirs if, burnt with the temple, they died upon the altars and hearths of their fathers. Titus had accomplished nothing; he had taken away little and given more. Paradise would take the temple’s place for them, and they, who had fought for God’s temple, would be transferred there, provided only that they did not see Roman triumphs with their own eyes or submit captive necks to the yoke. Their little children, whose parents had been champions of the heavenly mysteries, were being consecrated, not killed. Titus, all the more stirred to rescue at least those who were being held against their will, ordered the engines to be brought up.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.19.1] In the army was a son of Antiochus of Commagene, who had come to join in the war, an energetic young man indeed, ready in action but insufficiently provident in counsel. Thinking the Roman army’s restraint too slow, and not considering the difficulty of the task, he told Caesar that he wondered why the Romans hesitated to approach the wall. Titus laughed and said, “The task is for us all.” At these words the young man rushed forward with those whom he had armed in the Macedonian fashion and who were readier for battle. For he had come supported by others too, but the cohort called the Macedonian was thought to surpass the rest both in bodily strength and in its very stature. As they approached, the battle grew fiercer. Those on the wall fought back more readily, driven by extreme danger and encouraged by success in the present contest. The men below were pierced more often by those above, while not all their missiles reached the higher position. Yet the king’s son, eager in his youth, better protected by arms and more closely surrounded by his companions, evaded some blows and repelled others; his comrades’ warnings also instructed him how to avoid them, and so he remained free of wounds. But many of the Macedonian cohort were wounded as they fought more obstinately, because they thought it shameful to yield even to nature or fortifications. Thus, their attempt fruitless, they yielded to those above, having learnt that even Macedonian men, if they wished to conquer, needed both Alexander’s eagerness for battle and his good fortune in victory. For when he was besieging a city, while the others delayed and the army lingered over the customary engines, he energetically set up ladders, climbed the wall and, putting to flight those there who resisted from the wall, leapt alone into the city. There was no time for him, without a companion, to open the gates as dangers pressed upon him, but his unbounded spirit, eager for victory, sprang upon the enemy. Their ranks gave way, but how many could he strike down alone? Then the enemy poured round him through the various streets of the city. If Alexander pressed upon one side, he gave the others behind him the opportunity to surround him. So the conqueror kept turning his steps to avoid being surrounded by the people. But they had begun to press upon him in close array, and a great mass of weapons bristled over him. His helmet rang with clanging, his shield with the crash of stones. Had the Macedonians not burst in, fearing for their commander, the conqueror of innumerable nations would have been overwhelmed within a small city. It was therefore eagerness that made him leap upon the wall, cast down the enemy, rush alone into the city with a triumphal leap and put peoples to flight by his charge. Yet it was also good fortune, which a commander needs above all, that amid the onrush of so many peoples, so many shots of arrows and so many falling missiles, no place was found for a mortal wound. Valour had therefore brought danger, and eagerness would also have brought death, had good fortune deserted him as he fought. The Macedonians entered after breaking through the gate. Thus rashness found victory, and good fortune turned danger into glory. Our David too, while fighting against giants, was intent upon the enemy and had a killer behind him, but Abessa, the king’s companion, forestalled the man as he poised his blow. Yet good fortune saved Alexander, grace the prophet.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.20.1] Thus the son of Antiochus, king of Commagene, withdrew, learning that the Roman army’s considered restraint arose from caution, not fear, so that they might attack the wall with siege banks and shelters, battering rams and other engines. The banks were being built with the work divided among the units. Four principal banks had risen; one of them, opposite the stronghold named Antonia, had been carried through the middle of the pool they called Strutia. The fifth legion had made this bank thirty cubits high beside John’s tomb. Against these works John, the leader of the seditions, dug a tunnel underneath and left the Romans’ works hanging above it. The Romans did not know what the Jews had contrived in the hidden tunnel: they had kept its roof suspended by supports of planks and timber placed underneath, so that the whole deception remained concealed. Thus, when an opportunity presented itself, they applied fire. Fed by the sulphur and pitch with which the timber supporting the tunnel had been smeared, it easily consumed all the wood. The burning of the supports was followed by a collapse. The Romans’ works therefore suddenly fell with an enormous crash. Dust and smoke filled everything and spread deep darkness, while the hidden cause inspired greater terror. Then, when the other fuel which at first covered it had been consumed, the fire broke out freely and revealed the trick. The Romans’ fear of immediate danger diminished, but grievous weariness at their wasted labour took its place. At the same time no small shame tormented them because the Jews taunted them, and their hope of preparing a successful assault thereafter grew cold.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.20.2] In another part, two days later, when the wall was already being battered by a ram, Tepthaeus of Galilee and Magassarus, Adiabenus and Agiras seized torches and sprang upon the engines used against the walls. Nothing bolder than these men, nothing more terrible, advanced from the city against the enemy in that war. For, rushing into the midst of the enemy, they neither trembled nor drew back. Instead, as though lingering among their own friends, they thought they must not return, though javelins, arrows and missiles were hurled at them from every side, until they had set fire underneath and kindled the equipment of the siege engines. There was a great rush of the Roman army to extinguish the fire, and shouting and eager effort from the Jews too, devising obstacles for the Romans to prevent help being given. The Romans hurried to withdraw the rams from the flames; the Jews continued to spread fires. Thus, when everything that could burn had caught fire, the flames would have surrounded the Romans had they not acted promptly. For the Jews pressed fiercely, and their success fed their boldness precisely because their efforts in that part had not been fruitless. Indeed, no longer content with the protection of the walls, they advanced beyond them and attacked the Romans’ very guard posts. They had even gone forward to overthrow the fort in which the Romans kept watch. Had the glory of the Roman name and the ancient discipline of military service, which deterred men from abandoning such duties through fear of a graver penalty, not resisted the raging attackers, the very conquerors of cities would have yielded their own fortifications. Thus the appearance of the war and the practice of siege were reversed. The Romans defended themselves with catapults and missiles of the swifter kind, to repel the Jews by the same means with which they themselves had previously been resisted.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.20.3] Meanwhile Titus arrived, roused by the shouting and summoned to remedy the situation. The Romans immediately gained strength in Caesar’s presence, and shame nourished boldness. Titus cried out that it was a grievous disgrace to the Roman name if, with their roles reversed, they lost their own walls when they had already run out of enemy walls to overthrow. The Jews, distrusting their fortifications, relied on rashness alone; the Romans had only to stand firm, and victory would not fail them. Thus, by encouraging and fighting alike, Titus steadied his men and turned back the Jews, who were not only prepared in spirit for death but rushed forward with the very weight of their bodies to dislodge the Romans. Caesar’s danger was no small one amid the confusion of everything, when friend could not be distinguished from enemy. Titus moved in their midst, bold in his youth and the more eager to fight through his desire for glory, so that victory might be completed more quickly, placing concern for safety second to triumph.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.21.1] Yet, after the enemy had been driven back, counsel was divided. Some thought that the siege banks should be rebuilt and the engines for attacking the walls repaired. Others thought it wiser to withdraw from the dangers of the siege—there was no timber to rebuild the banks, and the danger was shared with the defeated—and enclose the city with a wall, so that hunger might destroy those deprived of supplies of food.

Others thought it wiser to withdraw from the dangers of the siege—there was no timber to rebuild the banks, and the danger was shared with the defeated—and enclose the city with a wall, so that hunger might destroy those deprived of supplies of food.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.21.2] This opinion prevailed: they were to be shut in so that they could not make unrestricted sorties and would be worn down all the more both by despair of escape and by lack of food. Thus, with portions of the work divided among the units, the wall rose swiftly, enclosing the city round its entire circuit. Caesar distributed duties among his men so that they would not omit their turns of guard duty at night either. In the first watch he himself undertook the duty of going round each rank of guards; he assigned the second watch to Alexander, and thereafter turns were entrusted to the tribunes in order, according to each man’s known diligence. Forts were set into the wall at intervals, and a band of soldiers kept watch in them; the sentries allotted themselves equal periods of sleep and watchfulness. At every moment they went round the wall, each from fort to fort over the distance prescribed for his duty. The night was kept busy by the successive turns of ranks and units.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.21.3] The Jews’ hope was cut off on every side, and hunger had poured in upon the enclosed people and descended into their very marrow. Everything resounded with the groans of those lamenting the torments of a pitiable death. Every place was filled with the half dead and, if you waited a little, with corpses. Within a moment those whom you had found alive failed. Those too who still breathed, worn away by wasting, bore the image of death, exhausted by hunger and ghastly with decay. They could scarcely even raise their eyes, because their substance, consumed by fasting, gave no vigour to natural movement. Only the human shape remained; its functions had perished. You would see images, but miss their activities. Dry skin clung to dry bones. If a slight movement disclosed a living person, the stench contradicted it, as did the wasted limbs and a colour so black that you would think it a shadow. Nor could the wretched be supplied with the offices of burial, since everyone was already exhausted and about to die. Even if more recent food gave someone a little strength, the heap of corpses had removed hope and made burial impossible for him. Many died while preparing the funerals of their own people, and by their own deaths left the duties of that final service incomplete. They fell upon the dead whom they had undertaken to cover, so that the man who had come to lighten the burden added himself to it, needing the ministry he was offering another. In the common calamity of all there was no room for grief, except that the authors of such great misery survived, nor time for complaint. Their voices were now free, if they could speak—for what could the dying still fear for themselves?—yet, with their senses already mute, they looked towards the temple, as though demanding from it vengeance for so dreadful an end. The tears of the last offices had dried up because the force of the evil had shut off every affection. The spirit had grown rigid; all feeling stood still in those enduring more than could be wept for. Ground for graves was now lacking, since every place within the city that could serve for burial had been dug up. Some tried to go out in the silence of night between the two walls, the enemy’s new one and the city’s old one; stealthy acts, dangerous but dutiful, had commended themselves to them. Thus, in place of one, several lay unburied, deprived of the service they had eagerly sought to offer one man as a good gift. But even where the enemy was absent, hunger did its work. The gravedigger often preceded the person to be buried, and was enclosed in the grave he had prepared for another. Suddenly lifeless and fallen while he dug, he claimed the right to his own work as though by deliberate intent. Where ground was lacking, boards were joined so that the bodies of the dead could be enclosed in coffins. Many prepared these for themselves with their own hands, lest this service fail them, and laid themselves in them of their own accord, fearing that death might forestall them and no gravedigger be available. Everything was silent with fear; starvation had taken away the voice. The city was full of death, and there was no wailing at the funeral of the whole city. Yet although the sense of grief had perished, injury did not cease. Even amid such great evils there were men worse than all the rest, who violated even the buried. What shall I say of their feeling no horror when they mocked the dead and tested the edges of their swords on lifeless bodies, while some even tried, by pressing them into the bodies of those still living, whether their weapons were very sharp? Yet this use too was denied to many who asked for it, so that hunger might devour the wretched for graver torments. Nevertheless, vengeance was by no means lacking for the dying. For what they had not been able to do alive, they did in death: they avenged themselves, creating a stench as their avenger, by which to take vengeance upon the brigands. Seeking a remedy for its grievous raging, even those who practised brigandage assumed a certain appearance of devotion and ordered the bodies to be buried at the expense of the public treasury. But when they could not keep pace, they threw the remains of the dead from the wall into the deep precipices.

paragraphs.rawText: [V.21.4] Thus Titus, seeing the steep chasms full of corpses and putrid matter floating among torn entrails, groaned deeply and raised his hands to heaven, declaring that this must by no means be ascribed to him: he had wished to grant pardon if surrender took place. He had waited for them to ask for peace and had been prepared to preserve them unharmed if they laid down war. He therefore ordered siege banks to be raised again, although the woods were no longer close at hand, because all the wooded groves near the city had been cut down. The soldiers carried timber, consoling their labour with the hope of victory. Yet the spirits of the leaders of sedition were not broken. Simon raged and did not yield, unsated by the deaths of so many; and because enemies had begun to run short, he turned upon his comrades.
