This has already been performed in the arenas of various cities, and ought to be shameful to us as an example or wretched as an experience: that we preserve ourselves to fight either beasts or brothers. Why then do we delay? We are no longer free to escape what we fear. If we are unwilling to kill our children out of mercy or ourselves through valour, we shall be compelled to kill our brothers or kinsmen in disgrace. The former affection urges; the latter the victors demand. If we are unwilling to perform the service of family devotion, we shall be forced to undergo the mockery of a pageant of the murder of kin. Let us therefore undertake what will benefit our children or wives. If they are weaker, let us remove them from the torments to come; if we are stronger, let us overcome parental compassion and the affections of kinship, and in this too conquer the enemy, whose booty we take away. Valour demands this, shame urges it. Not to fear death belongs to valour. For we are all born for death and beget children for death: their death is assigned to nature, their captivity counted as disgrace. Those whom we could not snatch from danger, therefore, let us snatch from mockery. Fathers, have mercy upon your children; husbands, upon your wives; all, upon the little ones. Let us have mercy, above all, upon ourselves while we have the power to show mercy, so that it may come from us, lest we seem both born and preserved for dishonour. For who could endure fathers killed before their sons’ faces and sons before their parents’ eyes, old men weary with grey age dragged away either to death or, worse, to slavery, women led away with dishevelled hair in their husbands’ sight and dragged by force to shame? Who could endure hearing the voice of a little child crying and calling his father to help him in his plea, when you now hear in vain, your hands bound and your captive neck beneath the yoke? Therefore, while our hands are still free, while we grasp the sword, let us undertake a work which the victorious enemy may admire. They themselves urge this; certainly those who wish it deserve it, and those who shrink from it must be compelled. Nor will the little ones fear the sword which, because of their age, they do not understand and which they ought to receive from devoted parents, so that they may truly become free. What could be more excellent for us too than to burn the stronghold first, yet preserve the grain, lest they think that we undertook the service of mutual slaughter compelled by hunger rather than invited by a desire for valour? We give them food filled with blood; and if the flames consume it, the very smell of the burning grain will show that what the besieged had in abundance was lost to the besiegers. paragraphs.runningText: Thus, with affairs desperate, Eleazar, the instigator of the disturbances, saw that no defence remained and began this speech. We have not omitted it, as a lamentable epilogue to close the work in the rhetorical manner: “What are we doing, men descended from Abraham, a royal race, invincible through the power of priestly grace? For valour is judged not by the outcome of victory, which is often uncertain, but by steadfastness of purpose. From this one may infer that subduing the enemy belongs to fortune, but not changing one’s mind belongs to valour. I may therefore rightly call you invincible if no fear of death has yet conquered you. But your father Abraham did not train you thus: in his only son he taught that, if he were sacrificed for religion, there would be not death but immortality for him. Why should I praise Josiah, than whom no one was a better interpreter of religion, despiser of death or champion of freedom? Placed on that royal eminence, he could have deferred death. Yet, because he saw that the captivity of the people of Israel would follow their grievous sins, he involved himself in another’s war and fled from life. Necho cried: ‘I have not been sent against you, but against the king of Israel.’ Yet Josiah did not withdraw before receiving a mortal arrow wound. Laid low by it, he shows us whether merit or chance carries greater weight in war. Josiah, the restorer of pious rites, was defeated; Necho, the most wicked of all men, won. But the defeated man is now with the angels, the victor in torment. For who does not know that the reward for human beings is stored up not in this life, but after this contest is completed? Here we run so that there we may reach the palm; here is the contest, there the reward. There is therefore no favour here in length of years. Indeed, Abel died early, Cain survived. Thus death fell to innocence and misery to life. Since then we have inherited the same lot: living has become most wretched, dying blessed. For what is life but a prison of the soul, which is shut within this slave-house and clings to companionship with the flesh? It is shaken by the body’s infirmities, afflicted by toil, crushed by anger, kindled by desires and harassed by fury. It cannot easily rise, bound to the ground, clotted with dust, fastened by a chain and entangled in sinews. Yet its power is no slight thing: it gives life to the body and pours the vigour of sense into insensible matter. Each person’s soul invisibly bestows this upon him, governs the whole man and carries him beyond mortal frailty, so that he may grasp the knowledge of heavenly secrets and direct his mind to the future. Thus, in the image and likeness of its ruler, it is not seen, though situated in the body. It is not perceived by bodily eyes, nor is its entry or departure caught by any gaze. Representing a certain likeness of the divine gift, it pours in life when it enters and brings about death when it leaves the body. Where the soul is, there is life; where it is absent, there is death. Whatever it visits it awakens; whatever it leaves is at once dissolved and immediately withers. By the soul’s infusion the dead man rises; by its departure the living man dies. Who then can doubt that immortality is seen to be at work in the soul, whose power is to avert death? Yet it is a burden to itself, though it abounds in service to another, and what it gives the body it takes away from itself. For it is weighed down and, as it were, bent towards the earth with this mortal body. Thus the body’s life is the soul’s death, and conversely the body’s death seems the soul’s freedom. For while we are in the body, our soul serves in slavery, a wretched slavery indeed, exiled from paradise and a stranger to its ruler. But when it is released from the bonds of this flesh, it flies back to that pure and shining place above, is present with the Lord its God, and enjoys the dwellings of the saints and the company of the blessed. It rejoices that it no longer has any fellowship with the dead and has left behind companionship with a corpse, that heavenly grace breathes upon it and no agitation of human cares troubles it. Sleep shows us how great a grace the soul resumes after the body’s death. For when the body sleeps and its desires and all its movements are as though dead, we often converse with the saints and receive those we have lost: the absent are present with us, the dead live, all grief is stilled, we approach God and converse with him, we know the future, the afflicted find rest and slaves freedom. What we dream in sleep we therefore attain in death; what is an image in sleep is in death the possession of truth and the grace of freedom. Hence some nations customarily greet people’s births with tears and their deaths with joy: they grieve that the former are born to misery and congratulate the latter on returning to blessedness; they lament that the souls of the former have come into slavery and rejoice that those of the latter have returned to freedom. The sages of the Indians too are said, when they have taken on the desire to die, to declare that they wish to depart, with no one raising a protest. Then, when the preparations for death have been made, they leap joyfully onto the burning pyre and bid farewell to those standing by. Women grieve as though about to be deprived of support, and little children because they are being left behind; others bless them and do not begrudge their hastening to better inhabitants, more splendid places and purer companions. I have long known you well and known you ready to answer to your ancestral institutions, holding that you should serve neither the Romans nor any nation, but God alone, who alone is the just and true Lord of all. The day has come which demands that you prove your will by deeds and not dishonour the splendour of your ancient character by subjecting yourselves, born in freedom, to human domination. You could previously have served without danger; now it is necessary to undergo harsh torments along with slavery if we offer ourselves to serve under Roman dominion, we who were the first of all to challenge them in war and the last still to hold them under arms. We did not surrender to the imperator when he offered peace; shall we surrender to Silva when he threatens cruelty? Wretched men, for what hope in this life shall we preserve ourselves? Granted, the enemy may pardon us. What will that avail when God’s offence is clear? The fires were turned from the enemy against us, the winds’ blasts changed, the flames bent back to burn our defences. Who can live with God opposed to him? paragraphs.rawText: [V.53.2] Fired by such a speech, the others held drawn swords, kissed their wives and embraced their children, weeping and hurrying at the same time to forestall the enemy. “These tokens of love,” he said, “we give you as consolation in the utmost necessity.” Manfully suppressing affection, they shut out feeling and carried out the slaughter. Fearless, the women offered themselves to the wound to preserve their chastity. They too had put on the minds of their husbands. After killing their kinsfolk and children, they chose vigorous men to complete the remaining slaughter. Thus all were laid low, nine hundred and sixty with the little ones and women. Only one woman survived; she hid five sons in an aqueduct while the others attended to their final necessities. Roused by the voices of the Romans arriving at daybreak, she told them what had happened. A fire which they themselves had previously set consumed their wealth.
